Here we propose and experimentally demonstrate a modified SR method, termed squeezing-induced SR, implemented in the system involving a trapped ion behaving as a Duffing oscillator. We find that squeezing the phase noise of the oscillator results in amplified fluctuation of the corresponding amplitude, which helps achieve the SR. Since no auxiliary noise source is needed, the squeezing-induced SR may enhance the signal-to-noise ratio by 4.28 $\pm$ 0.39 dB compared to the conventional noise-induced SR under identical conditions of the electric-field detection. This technique offers a promising approach for developing atomic ion sensors for detecting weak electric-field signals.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and demonstrates squeezing-induced stochastic resonance (SR) using a trapped ion Duffing oscillator, achieving signal-to-noise ratio enhancement of 4.28 ± 0.39 dB over conventional noise-induced SR without needing auxiliary noise sources.
AI.motivation: To overcome the need for external noise sources in conventional stochastic resonance and improve weak electric-field signal detection in nonlinear systems.
AI.method: A modified SR method called squeezing-induced SR is implemented in a trapped ion system behaving as a Duffing oscillator, where phase noise squeezing amplifies amplitude fluctuations to achieve resonance.
AI.result: Squeezing-induced SR improves signal-to-noise ratio by 4.28 ± 0.39 dB compared to conventional noise-induced SR under identical electric-field detection conditions.
AI.conclusion: This technique provides a promising approach for developing atomic ion sensors capable of detecting weak electric-field signals without requiring auxiliary noise sources.

title: Berry-phase in a periodically driven single molecule magnet transistor
summary: We consider the electron transport through a single molecule magnet transistor in the presence of a local transverse magnetic field and ac-driven gate voltage. We calculate the conductance as a function of the electron energy and transverse magnetic field by using the Floquet and Landauer formalism. We show that the time periodic potential causes zero transmission resonances that oscillate as a function of the transverse magnetic field due to the Berry phase interference associated with two quantum tunneling paths. We find that these Berry phase oscillations can be detected in the conductance as a function of the transverse magnetic field for an incoming electron with a specific energy.

AI.tldr: This paper studies electron transport through a single molecule magnet transistor under a transverse magnetic field and ac-driven gate voltage, revealing Berry phase interference oscillations in conductance due to time-periodic potential causing zero transmission resonances.
AI.motivation: To understand how electron transport through a single molecule magnet transistor is affected by the combined influence of a transverse magnetic field and an ac-driven gate voltage, particularly focusing on the role of Berry phase interference.
AI.method: The Floquet and Landauer formalisms are used to calculate conductance as a function of electron energy and transverse magnetic field.
AI.result: The time-periodic potential induces zero transmission resonances that oscillate with the transverse magnetic field due to Berry phase interference from two quantum tunneling paths.
AI.conclusion: Berry phase oscillations can be observed in the conductance as a function of the transverse magnetic field for incoming electrons with specific energies.

title: Incommensurate Antiferromagnetic Order in the Fe-substituted Bi-2201 Cuprate in the Heavily Overdoped Regime
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, J. Phys. Soc. Jpn., in press
summary: Elastic neutron scattering experiments showed incommensurate antiferromagnetic peaks in 5% Fe-substituted Bi-2201 cuprate in the non-superconducting heavily overdoped regime. The incommensurability delta~0.21 is comparable to that observed in Fe-substituted Bi-2201 in the overdoped regime. [Hiraka et al., Phys. Rev. B 81, 144501 (2010).] The magnetic correlation length is comparable between the overdoped and non-superconducting heavily overdoped regimes. It is plausible that incommensurate antiferromagnetic order is induced and stabilized by Fe in the heavily overdoped regime, which suggests a robust antiferromagnetic correlation beyond the superconducting dome in the phase diagram.

AI.tldr: Elastic neutron scattering reveals incommensurate antiferromagnetic peaks in 5% Fe-substituted Bi-2201 cuprate in the non-superconducting heavily overdoped regime, with incommensurability δ~0.21 and magnetic correlation length comparable to overdoped samples, suggesting robust antiferromagnetic correlations persist beyond the superconducting dome.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether antiferromagnetic correlations persist beyond the superconducting dome in heavily overdoped cuprates, using Fe-substituted Bi-2201 as a probe.
AI.method: Elastic neutron scattering experiments on 5% Fe-substituted Bi-2201 cuprate in the non-superconducting heavily overdoped regime.
AI.result: Incommensurate antiferromagnetic peaks were observed with incommensurability δ~0.21, comparable to overdoped Fe-substituted Bi-2201. The magnetic correlation length is similar between overdoped and heavily overdoped regimes.
AI.conclusion: Fe likely induces and stabilizes incommensurate antiferromagnetic order in the heavily overdoped regime, indicating robust antiferromagnetic correlations that survive beyond the superconducting dome in the phase diagram.

title: Machine Learning Approaches to Point Defects in Non-Metallic Materials: A Review of Methods
summary: We review recent machine-learning (ML) approaches for point defects in non-metallic materials, with an emphasis on defect formation energies. Existing studies largely fall into two categories: direct ML models that predict defect energetics from local structural representations, and machine-learning potentials (MLPs) that approximate the defect-containing potential energy surface. We summarize key achievements as well as persistent bottlenecks, emphasizing that dataset quality often dominates practical model performance. We further identify charged-defect formation energies as a central frontier, where Fermi-level alignment, finite-size corrections, and long-range electrostatics must be handled carefully and consistently to enable meaningful comparisons and transferable predictions across different materials.

AI.tldr: A review of ML approaches for point defects in non-metallic materials, covering direct ML models and machine-learning potentials, with charged-defect formation energies identified as a key frontier requiring careful handling of electrostatics and corrections.
AI.motivation: To systematically review recent ML approaches for predicting point defect properties in non-metallic materials, highlighting progress and persistent challenges, particularly for charged defects where electrostatic effects complicate predictions.
AI.method: The review categorizes existing studies into two types: (1) direct ML models that predict defect energetics from local structural representations, and (2) machine-learning potentials (MLPs) that approximate the potential energy surface of defect-containing systems.
AI.result: Dataset quality often dominates practical model performance. Charged-defect formation energies remain a central frontier requiring careful Fermi-level alignment, finite-size corrections, and long-range electrostatic handling.
AI.conclusion: Meaningful comparisons and transferable predictions across different materials for charged defects require consistent treatment of electrostatic corrections and alignment strategies.

title: Systematic dynamical mean-field theory study of 3d perovskite oxides with uniform Coulomb interactions
summary: Strongly correlated transition-metal perovskite oxides pose a fundamental challenge for electronic-structure theory and for large-scale, data-driven materials discovery. While DFT+DMFT provides a quantitatively accurate description of such systems, its high-throughput application is hindered by the need to determine material-specific Coulomb interaction parameters ($U$). First-principles approaches such as the cRPA predict a highly nonlinear and non-transferable evolution of the interaction strength across chemically similar ABO$_3$ perovskites. Here we show that this paradigm does not extend to the large-energy-window eDMFT, which employs highly localized orbitals and treats electronic correlations and screening self-consistently within the same many-body framework. As a result, spectral properties are governed primarily by the dynamical self-energy rather than by static interaction-induced energy shifts. Recent constrained-eDMFT calculations demonstrated that, for broad classes of $3d$ transition-metal oxides, the self-consistently screened Coulomb interactions naturally fall within relatively narrow ranges for correlated metals and insulators. Motivated by these findings, we implement a high-throughput eDMFT framework employing physically derived interaction values of $U=6$ eV for metals and $U=10$ eV for insulators together with $exact$ double counting. We test this framework using systematic high-throughput eDMFT calculations for ABO$_3$ compounds (A = Ca, Sr, La; B = V--Ni) and benchmark the resulting spectral functions against photoemission experiments, where we find overall excellent agreement. Our results establish that charge self-consistent eDMFT enables robust, parameter-tuning-free high-throughput many-body calculations for correlated oxides, opening a practical pathway toward predictive electronic-structure databases for strongly correlated materials.

AI.tldr: High-throughput eDMFT calculations for strongly correlated perovskites are achieved using fixed, physically derived Coulomb interaction values (U=6 eV for metals, U=10 eV for insulators) with exact double counting, bypassing the need for material-specific U determination, and yield excellent agreement with photoemission experiments across ABO3 compounds.
AI.motivation: Strongly correlated transition-metal perovskites are challenging for electronic-structure theory and high-throughput materials discovery because DFT+DMFT requires material-specific Coulomb interaction parameters (U) that are costly to compute and exhibit nonlinear, non-transferable behavior across chemically similar compounds.
AI.method: The authors implement a high-throughput charge self-consistent eDMFT framework using fixed U values (6 eV for metals, 10 eV for insulators) with exact double counting, and systematically test it on ABO3 perovskites (A=Ca, Sr, La; B=V–Ni).
AI.result: The self-consistently screened Coulomb interactions in eDMFT fall within narrow ranges across broad classes of 3d transition-metal oxides. Using fixed U values, spectral functions show excellent agreement with photoemission experiments for the tested ABO3 compounds.
AI.conclusion: Charge self-consistent eDMFT enables robust, parameter-tuning-free high-throughput many-body calculations for correlated oxides, paving the way for predictive electronic-structure databases for strongly correlated materials.

title: Irreversibility from Self-Reference: Gradient Flow and an H-Theorem for a Self-Referential Statistical Operator Framework
summary: This paper is a direct companion to arXiv:2605.06705, where the self-referential operator Omega was introduced and the Tsallis index q = alpha + beta was derived as a fixed-point condition within the local kernel approximation (LKA). Here we address four aspects deferred from the previous work. First, we carry out the first-order perturbative expansion of Omega beyond the LKA and demonstrate structural stability of q = alpha + beta at leading order in (xi/L)^2. Second, we define the iterative dynamical scheme Psi_(n+1) = Omega[Psi_n] and analyze convergence via Frechet spectral radius. Third, and centrally, we establish an H-theorem rigorously within the LKA for both the discrete iteration and the continuous gradient flow: we compute dF/dtau explicitly along the flow, identify the negative semi-definite dissipation term, establish the result rigorously in the LKA using strict convexity of F proved in the companion paper, and provide numerical evidence showing monotone decrease of F[Psi_n] across 53 iterations on an N = 80 discrete system. Fourth, we characterize the non-perturbative role of the self-coupling parameter kappa, identifying a re-entrant disordered phase at kappa > kappa* approximately 0.50 +/- 0.05. The paper is explicit about what is proved, what is established numerically, and what open problems remain for a complete analytical proof beyond the LKA.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the theoretical framework of the self-referential operator Omega (introduced in companion paper arXiv:2605.06705) by: (1) performing first-order perturbative expansion beyond the local kernel approximation (LKA) to confirm structural stability of the Tsallis index q = alpha + beta; (2) defining and analyzing convergence of the iterative dynamical scheme Psi_(n+1) = Omega[Psi_n] via Frechet spectral radius; (3) establishing an H-theorem within the LKA for both discrete iteration and continuous gradient flow with rigorous proof and numerical evidence; (4) characterizing the non-perturbative role of self-coupling parameter kappa, identifying a re-entrant disordered phase at kappa > kappa* ~ 0.50 ± 0.05.
AI.motivation: To address four aspects deferred from the companion paper: go beyond the LKA to verify structural stability of the derived Tsallis index, define and analyze convergence of the iterative dynamics, prove an H-theorem for monotonic dissipation, and characterize the non-perturbative role of kappa including re-entrant disorder.
AI.method: First-order perturbative expansion of Omega beyond LKA at order (xi/L)^2; Frechet spectral radius analysis for the iterative scheme Psi_(n+1) = Omega[Psi_n]; rigorous H-theorem derivation within LKA for both discrete iteration and continuous gradient flow using strict convexity of F; numerical simulation across 53 iterations on N=80 discrete system; phase characterization via kappa parameter scan.
AI.result: Structural stability of q = alpha + beta at leading order in (xi/L)^2; identification of negative semi-definite dissipation term in the H-theorem; numerical monotonic decrease of F[Psi_n] over 53 iterations; identification of re-entrant disordered phase at kappa > kappa* ≈ 0.50 ± 0.05.
AI.conclusion: The work provides rigorous results within the LKA and perturbative extensions beyond it, with open problems remaining for complete analytical proof outside the LKA regime.

title: Data-driven analysis of metastability in a stochastic bistable system
summary: We study the metastability properties of a simple prototypical bistable system using the formalism of the Koopman operator. Instead of studying noise-induced transitions by following the trajectories of the system, we track them by studying the time evolution and the decay rate of the subdominant mode of the Koopman operator, thus in a geometry-agnostic framework. We find agreement with the predictions - both the exponential and subexponential ones - of large deviation theory in the weak-noise limit for the statistics of escape time, both in equilibrium and nonequilibrium conditions. The subdominant Koopman mode also allows for an accurate reconstruction of the competing basins of attraction. Going deeper in the Koopman spectrum, we are able to recognise modes that are associated with intrawell variability as well as with the escape of trajectories from the saddle towards the attractor, both in the equilibrium and nonequilibrium case. Our methodology, being grounded in purely data-driven techniques, could be helpful for studying high-dimensional metastable systems.

AI.tldr: This paper uses Koopman operator theory to study metastability in a bistable system, showing that the subdominant Koopman mode captures noise-induced transitions and escape statistics consistent with large deviation theory, while also enabling reconstruction of basins of attraction and identification of intrawell and saddle-escape dynamics.
AI.motivation: To develop a geometry-agnostic, data-driven framework for studying metastability and noise-induced transitions in bistable systems, avoiding trajectory-based methods.
AI.method: The authors apply Koopman operator formalism to analyze the subdominant mode's time evolution and decay rate, comparing escape time statistics with large deviation theory predictions (both exponential and subexponential) under equilibrium and nonequilibrium conditions.
AI.result: The subdominant Koopman mode agrees with large deviation theory predictions for escape time statistics in the weak-noise limit, accurately reconstructs competing basins of attraction, and reveals modes corresponding to intrawell variability and saddle-to-attractor escape trajectories.
AI.conclusion: The Koopman-based methodology provides a purely data-driven, geometry-agnostic approach that could be useful for studying high-dimensional metastable systems.

title: Finite-frequency anomaly-induced electromechanical response of Dirac fermions in deformed graphene
summary: A deformation of a graphene sheet changes more than the positions of the atoms. In the low-energy Dirac theory it also produces geometric electron-phonon vertices. One of these vertices acts as an emergent phonon gauge field, $\calA_μ$, which couples to the same Dirac current as the electromagnetic vector potential. This shared current vertex gives a direct route from mechanics to electronics: a moving deformation can generate a transverse electric current, and a deformation pattern with emergent phonon flux can bind electric charge. We show that the coefficient of this mixed electromechanical response is the parity-odd current-current correlator of a massive Dirac cone. For an insulating cone the coefficient is the one-cone Chern-Simons value, while for a doped cone in the local regime it is reduced by the Berry curvature factor $m/|μ|$. We apply the response to explicit deformations. A traveling flexural wave generates a transverse second-harmonic current; a static ripple mixed with a dynamic phonon generates a transverse current at the drive frequency; and two non-collinear modes can generate charge modulation through the emergent phonon flux. We keep the spin and valley sum explicit, so the paper shows when the one-cone anomaly becomes a charge current in graphene and when it instead appears in a valley, spin, or spin-valley channel. For sublattice-gapped graphene with a valley-odd deformation gauge coupling, the two valleys add rather than cancel. The experimentally sharp signature is a transverse electrical signal at twice the flexural-wave frequency, with a phase fixed by the sign of the sublattice gap and a gate dependence that crosses over from a gap plateau to a $1/|μ|$ decay. These direction, phase, frequency, and gate-voltage selection rules give clean tests of the anomaly-induced electromechanical channel in deformed graphene.

AI.tldr: Moving deformations in graphene generate electric currents and charge via a phonon gauge field coupling, with sharp experimental signatures like transverse second-harmonic current from flexural waves, depending on sublattice gap and doping.
AI.motivation: To understand how mechanical deformations in graphene produce electrical responses (currents and charge) via emergent phonon gauge fields in the Dirac theory, and to identify clean experimental signatures of this anomaly-induced electromechanical coupling.
AI.method: Derives the coefficient of mixed electromechanical response from the parity-odd current-current correlator of a massive Dirac cone. Analyzes explicit deformations: traveling flexural wave, static ripple with dynamic phonon, and non-collinear modes. Keeps spin and valley sums explicit to distinguish charge, valley, spin, and spin-valley channels.
AI.result: The response coefficient is the Chern-Simons value for insulating cones and reduced by Berry curvature factor m/|μ| for doped cones. Flexural wave generates transverse second-harmonic current; static ripple+dynamic phonon gives transverse current at drive frequency; non-collinear modes produce charge modulation. For sublattice-gapped graphene with valley-odd coupling, valleys add instead of cancel.
AI.conclusion: The predicted transverse electrical signal at twice flexural-wave frequency, with phase fixed by sublattice gap sign and gate-dependent crossover from gap plateau to 1/|μ| decay, provides clean experimental tests (direction, phase, frequency, gate-voltage selection rules) of the anomaly-induced electromechanical channel in deformed graphene.

title: Chemical Interpretation of Time-Dependent Coupled-Cluster Theory
summary: While providing a highly accurate framework for simulating laser-induced many-electron dynamics in atom and molecules, including linear and nonlinear steady-state and transient absorption spectra, time-dependent coupled-cluster theory does not offer a straightforward interpretation in chemical terms. This should be contrasted with conventional time-independent equation-of-motion coupled-cluster or frequency-dependent response models where a simple eigenvector analysis readily reveals the dominant orbital-excitation character of individual excited states. We fill this gap by expanding the left and right coupled-cluster functions in Slater-determinant basis, thus allowing for a time-dependent generalization of configuration weights that can be used to track populations throughout a simulation. The same expansions are used to decompose the time-dependent electric-dipole moment and autocorrelation function, providing a computationally straightforward approach to the assignment of absorption peaks to orbital transitions for single-reference systems. At the time-dependent coupled-cluster singles-and-doubles level of theory, we demonstrate the power of the proposed methodology by assigning valence lines in the linear absorption spectra of four ten-electron molecules (HF, H2O, NH3, and CH4) with different point-group symmetries, validating the assignment by comparison with equation-of-motion coupled-cluster singles-and-doubles theory. In addition, core-level excitations are assigned for HF, H2O, and NH3. Finally, the usefulness of time-dependent configuration weights is illustrated by applications to an impulsive stimulated x-ray Raman scattering process in the Ne atom and to a transient pump-probe spectrum of the HF molecule.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a method to interpret time-dependent coupled-cluster (TDCC) simulations in chemical terms by expanding CC functions in Slater-determinant basis, enabling configuration weight tracking and decomposition of time-dependent properties for assigning absorption peaks to orbital transitions.
AI.motivation: Time-dependent coupled-cluster theory lacks straightforward chemical interpretation (e.g., orbital-excitation character of excited states), unlike conventional time-independent equation-of-motion or response CC models where eigenvector analysis provides such insight.
AI.method: The method expands left and right CC functions in Slater-determinant basis to obtain time-dependent configuration weights, and similarly decomposes the time-dependent electric-dipole moment and autocorrelation function. Implemented at the TDCC singles-and-doubles (TDCCSD) level.
AI.result: Demonstrated on four ten-electron molecules (HF, H2O, NH3, CH4) for valence line assignment validated against EOM-CCSD; also assigned core-level excitations for HF, H2O, NH3; further illustrated on impulsive stimulated X-ray Raman scattering in Ne and transient pump-probe spectrum of HF.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methodology successfully bridges the interpretability gap between time-dependent CC theory and conventional frequency-domain CC models, providing a computationally efficient way to assign spectral features to orbital transitions in single-reference systems.

title: SPARC-atomSFE: Spectral finite-element package for atomic structure calculations in density functional theory
summary: We present SPARC-atomSFE, a spectral finite-element package for accurate and efficient atomic structure calculations within the framework of Kohn-Sham density functional theory. The package supports both all-electron and norm conserving pseudopotential calculations across a comprehensive hierarchy of exchange-correlation approximations, spanning local, semilocal, and nonlocal functionals. The latter includes hybrid functionals and the many-body random phase approximation, for which we implement both the generalized Kohn-Sham approach and the optimized effective potential (OEP) method, with OEP necessary for eigenvalue-dependent functionals. Spatial discretization is based on an adaptive grid with element nodes distributed according to the Legendre--Gauss--Lobatto scheme, high-order $C^{0}$-continuous Lagrange polynomial basis functions, and Gauss--Legendre quadrature for numerical integration. We present systematic convergence studies and identify the computational parameters required to achieve target accuracies. We validate the accuracy of SPARC-atomSFE through representative calculations spanning the various exchange-correlations approximations, obtaining results that generally agree with values in the literature to within $1~μ\text{Ha}$ or better.

AI.tldr: SPARC-atomSFE is a spectral finite-element package for atomic structure calculations in Kohn-Sham DFT, supporting all-electron and pseudopotential methods with various exchange-correlation functionals (local to hybrid/RPA), using adaptive spectral-element grids with high-order Lagrange polynomials, validated to sub-μHa accuracy.
AI.motivation: To provide an accurate and efficient computational package for atomic structure calculations within DFT that can handle a wide hierarchy of exchange-correlation approximations, including hybrid functionals and RPA, with systematic convergence control and high precision.
AI.method: Spectral finite-element method with adaptive grid, Legendre-Gauss-Lobatto node distribution, high-order C0-continuous Lagrange polynomials, and Gauss-Legendre quadrature; supports all-electron and norm-conserving pseudopotential approaches; implements both generalized Kohn-Sham and optimized effective potential (OEP) methods for nonlocal/eigenvalue-dependent functionals.
AI.result: Systematic convergence studies identified parameters needed for target accuracies; validation across multiple exchange-correlation approximations showed agreement with literature values to within 1 μHa or better.
AI.conclusion: SPARC-atomSFE achieves high accuracy (sub-μHa) for atomic structure calculations across a broad range of DFT functionals, with reliable convergence behavior.

title: Switching Rydberg interactions by three orders of magnitude using a terahertz field
comment: 4 pages with 4 figures plus two pages supplemental material
summary: Atom-based quantum computing exploits the ability to enhance atom-atom interactions by employing laser excitation to higher-excited Rydberg states. Additional fields that drive transitions between Rydberg states can offer independent control of these atom-atom interactions. However, as microwave (mw) fields only provide access to states with similar principal quantum number $n$, their ability to switch the interactions' strength is limited. Here, we use a pulsed terahertz field to rapidly switch the strength of interactions between Rydberg atoms by three orders of magnitude. We demonstrate interaction switching using photon storage, where the terahertz field induces an interaction induced dephasing of the stored photon. This ability to switch interactions offers advantages for single-qubit readout, state-detection schemes, quantum annealing, and Rydberg quantum optics.

AI.tldr: Researchers use pulsed terahertz fields to rapidly switch Rydberg atom interaction strength by three orders of magnitude, demonstrated via interaction-induced dephasing of stored photons.
AI.motivation: Existing microwave-based methods for controlling Rydberg atom interactions are limited because they can only access states with similar principal quantum numbers, restricting the ability to switch interaction strength.
AI.method: A pulsed terahertz field is applied to rapidly switch the interaction strength between Rydberg atoms. The switching is demonstrated through photon storage experiments where the terahertz field induces interaction-induced dephasing.
AI.result: The terahertz field switches Rydberg atom interaction strength by three orders of magnitude, enabling rapid modulation from weak to strong interactions.
AI.conclusion: This terahertz-based interaction switching offers advantages for single-qubit readout, state-detection schemes, quantum annealing, and Rydberg quantum optics.

title: Emergent impedance due to antiferromagnetic domain wall dynamics
summary: We theoretically investigate emergent impedance induced by domain-wall dynamics in antiferromagnets. Emergent impedance, arising from a combined action of spin-transfer torque and spinmotive force, was previously predicted and observed in spiral magnets. Here we develop a formalism for the electrical response of an antiferromagnetic domain wall under ac currents, and obtain analytical expressions for the resulting emergent impedance. We find that two dynamical modes play separate roles in the emergent impedance: Translational motion of the domain-wall center generates a contribution proportional to its velocity, analogous to that arising from the corresponding motion of a spiral magnet. Another contribution, unique to antiferromagnetic domain walls, originates from the time-dependent canting of the sublattice magnetizations localized within the moving domain wall, whose magnitude is inversely proportional to the antiferromagnetic exchange coupling constant. The competition between these two distinct contributions determines the sign and magnitude of the imaginary part of the emergent impedance at sub-resonant frequencies. Our results provide a fundamental insight into electron transport in antiferromagnets, and open avenues for novel antiferromagnet-based spintronics devices.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically investigates emergent impedance in antiferromagnetic domain walls under AC currents, identifying two contributions: one from translational motion (analogous to spiral magnets) and a unique contribution from time-dependent canting of sublattice magnetizations within the moving domain wall, inversely proportional to exchange coupling. The competition determines the sign and magnitude of the imaginary impedance at sub-resonant frequencies.
AI.motivation: To develop a formalism for the electrical response of antiferromagnetic domain walls under AC currents and understand the emergent impedance mechanisms, extending previous work on spiral magnets to antiferromagnetic systems.
AI.method: Theoretical formalism combining spin-transfer torque and spinmotive force effects to derive analytical expressions for emergent impedance in antiferromagnetic domain walls under AC currents.
AI.result: Two dynamical modes contribute: (1) translational motion of the domain-wall center (velocity-proportional, analogous to spiral magnets), and (2) time-dependent canting of sublattice magnetizations within the moving domain wall (unique to antiferromagnets, inversely proportional to exchange coupling). Their competition determines the imaginary impedance sign and magnitude at sub-resonant frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Provides fundamental insight into electron transport in antiferromagnets and opens avenues for novel antiferromagnet-based spintronics devices.

title: Bogoliubov sum rules and the Knight-shift ellipsoid in noncentrosymmetric superconductors
summary: We show that the residual $T=0$ Knight shift of a noncentrosymmetric superconductor in the strong-locking regime is completely determined by a single Fermi-surface average -- the projector $Π_{μν}=\langle\hat n_μ\hat n_ν\rangle_{\rm FS}$ of the spin-locking direction $\hat n_{\mathbf{k}}$ -- giving the tensor identity $χ_{μν}(0)=χ_{N}[δ_{μν}-Π_{μν}]$ independently of pairing symmetry, gap magnitude, and Fermi-surface shape. Because $\mathrm{Tr}\,Π=1$, the three principal Knight shifts at $T=0$ lie on a two-dimensional simplex of locking textures, the \emph{Knight-shift ellipsoid}, whose vertices, edges, and interior classify every canonical pairing class. The identity follows from a Bogoliubov sum rule, $\sum|M_{ph,O}|^{2}+\sum|M_{pp,O}|^{2}=\mathrm{Tr}_{s}(O^{2})$, valid at every momentum for every Hermitian single-particle operator $O$ as the BdG-doubled form of unitary invariance. Around the central theorem we develop controlled departures (a closed-form $s$-wave SOC interpolation, a finite-field strong-locking identity), a dynamical counterpart (a spin Ferrell--Glover--Tinkham sum rule and a rigorous vanishing-projection theorem for $1/T_{1}$), and a decoupled-pocket multiband baseline, packaged into six experimental protocols. Applied to the $^{75}$As NMR data on K$_{2}$Cr$_{3}$As$_{3}$, the observed ellipsoid sits at the oblate-axial vertex $(0,0,1)$ and saturates the trace bound; the decoupled-pocket SOC-texture baseline is excluded by $\sim 0.5$ in normalized units, requiring a common $\hat c$-axis locking on all three pockets, and the suppression of $1/T_{1}\parallel\hat c$ is identified, via the vanishing-projection theorem, as a fingerprint of finite-$\mathbf{q}$ ferromagnetic spin-fluctuation gap formation.

AI.tldr: The residual T=0 Knight shift in noncentrosymmetric superconductors in the strong-locking regime is determined solely by the Fermi-surface average of the spin-locking direction projector, yielding a universal tensor identity independent of pairing symmetry, gap magnitude, and Fermi-surface shape. This leads to a Knight-shift ellipsoid classification of pairing classes, derived from a Bogoliubov sum rule, with applications to K₂Cr₃As₃ NMR data revealing c-axis locking and ferromagnetic spin-fluctuation gap formation.
AI.motivation: To derive a universal, pairing-independent expression for the residual T=0 Knight shift in noncentrosymmetric superconductors with strong spin-orbit locking, classify pairing textures via a geometric ellipsoid framework, and provide experimentally testable protocols applied to real materials like K₂Cr₃As₃.
AI.method: The authors derive a tensor identity χ_μν(0) = χ_N[δ_μν - Π_μν] from a Bogoliubov sum rule ∑|M_ph,O|² + ∑|M_pp,O|² = Tr_s(O²). They analyze the Fermi-surface average of the spin-locking direction projector Π_μν = ⟨n̂_μ n̂_ν⟩_FS, classify pairing classes on a Knight-shift ellipsoid simplex, and develop controlled departures including s-wave SOC interpolation, finite-field identities, dynamical sum rules, and multiband decoupled-pocket baselines.
AI.result: The three principal Knight shifts lie on a two-dimensional simplex (Knight-shift ellipsoid) with vertices, edges, and interior classifying canonical pairing classes. Applied to ⁷⁵As NMR on K₂Cr₃As₃, the observed ellipsoid sits at the oblate-axial vertex (0,0,1), saturates the trace bound, excludes a decoupled-pocket SOC-texture baseline by ~0.5 in normalized units, and the suppression of 1/T₁ ∥ ĉ is identified as a fingerprint of finite-q ferromagnetic spin-fluctuation gap formation.
AI.conclusion: The residual Knight shift in strong-locking noncentrosymmetric superconductors is universal and independent of pairing details, governed solely by the spin-locking texture's Fermi-surface average. This yields a geometric classification scheme and six experimental protocols, with K₂Cr₃As₃ data confirming common c-axis locking across all pockets and revealing ferromagnetic spin-fluctuation gap formation.

title: Non-linear diffusion and inhomogeneity of the magnetic field in single-turn coils: Insights from 3D multiphysics modeling
summary: The single-turn coil method is a destructive pulsed magnet for generating over 100 T with a few $μ$-second pulse duration, and it inevitably causes the coil to explode. The temporal and spatial distributions of the electric current and magnetic field are highly inhomogeneous, arising from the skin effect, rapid temperature rise, and coil deformation. To grasp the dynamic phenomena in the single-turn coil, we conducted a finite element analysis using multiphysics simulation. We employed finite element method calculations using a fully 3D model of the single-turn coil with broken cylindrical symmetry. The calculated result revealed highly nonlinear diffusion of electric current, temperature, and magnetic fields, which are the sources of the inhomogeneous magnetic fields inside the single-turn coil in time and space.

AI.tldr: A multiphysics finite element analysis of the single-turn coil method reveals highly nonlinear diffusion of electric current, temperature, and magnetic fields, explaining the inhomogeneous temporal and spatial magnetic field distributions inside the coil during destructive pulsed magnet operation.
AI.motivation: To understand the dynamic phenomena (skin effect, rapid temperature rise, coil deformation) in the single-turn coil method that cause inhomogeneous electric current and magnetic field distributions, and to enable better generation of over 100 T destructive pulsed magnetic fields.
AI.method: Finite element analysis using multiphysics simulation with a fully 3D model of the single-turn coil, accounting for broken cylindrical symmetry.
AI.result: The simulation revealed highly nonlinear diffusion of electric current, temperature, and magnetic fields, which are the sources of inhomogeneous magnetic fields inside the single-turn coil both in time and space.
AI.conclusion: The inhomogeneous temporal and spatial distributions of electric current and magnetic fields in the single-turn coil method arise from coupled nonlinear phenomena including skin effect, rapid heating, and coil deformation, as demonstrated by 3D multiphysics finite element modeling.

title: Finite-Temperature Spin Exchange-Correlation Kernel of the Uniform Electron Gas
summary: The finite-temperature spin response of the uniform electron gas (UEG) is a fundamental reference for spin-polarized and magnetized electron liquids, including warm dense matter (WDM), yet it remains far less constrained than charge response. Using variational diagrammatic Monte Carlo, we compute the static spin exchange--correlation (XC) kernel $K_{xc}(q;T)$ of the unpolarized UEG at metallic densities across the quantum-degenerate, warm-dense, and classical regimes. The kernel connects smoothly to zero-temperature spin-response parametrizations at low temperature, while heating suppresses the Fermi-surface-scale spin-correlation structure and weakens the XC-driven Stoner enhancement. Its long-wavelength limit provides a direct response test of the spin stiffness implied by thermal local-spin-density-approximation (LSDA) parametrizations, showing low-temperature consistency while exposing a resolved warm-dense residual in current LSDA parametrizations. In the classical regime, the spin XC kernel becomes nearly local on the Fermi-momentum scale, in sharp contrast to the corresponding charge XC kernel. These results provide a first-principles basis for finite-temperature spin-response theory and magnetized WDM modeling.

AI.tldr: Using variational diagrammatic Monte Carlo, the paper computes the static spin exchange-correlation kernel of the uniform electron gas across quantum-degenerate, warm-dense, and classical regimes, revealing smooth low-temperature connection to zero-temperature parametrizations, heating-induced suppression of spin correlation, and a resolved warm-dense residual in current LSDA parametrizations, with the classical spin kernel becoming nearly local on the Fermi-momentum scale.
AI.motivation: The finite-temperature spin response of the uniform electron gas is a fundamental reference for spin-polarized and magnetized electron liquids (including warm dense matter), yet it remains far less constrained than charge response.
AI.method: Variational diagrammatic Monte Carlo is used to compute the static spin exchange-correlation kernel K_xc(q;T) of the unpolarized UEG at metallic densities across quantum-degenerate, warm-dense, and classical regimes.
AI.result: (1) Smooth connection to zero-temperature spin-response parametrizations at low temperature. (2) Heating suppresses Fermi-surface-scale spin-correlation structure and weakens XC-driven Stoner enhancement. (3) Long-wavelength limit shows low-temperature consistency with thermal LSDA parametrizations but exposes a resolved warm-dense residual in current LSDA parametrizations. (4) In the classical regime, the spin XC kernel becomes nearly local on the Fermi-momentum scale, contrasting sharply with the charge XC kernel.
AI.conclusion: These results provide a first-principles basis for finite-temperature spin-response theory and magnetized warm dense matter modeling.

title: The problem of relaxation to equilibrium
comment: Number of pages: 7 Number of figures: 5
summary: When a thermodynamic system is released from any constraint, after some time its evolution will render it into an equilibrium state. Although the description of this relaxation to thermodynamic equilibrium has been attempted through both classical (Hamilton's equations) or quantum (Schrödinger equation) approaches, no success has been achieved without recurring to additional hypotheses. The present work demonstrates the possibility of reaching equilibrium states in a simple classical gaseous system, by imposing non-strict boundary conditions, in the sense that all interactions with the container walls must occur according to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that a classical gaseous system can reach thermodynamic equilibrium by applying Heisenberg's uncertainty principle to particle-wall interactions, without needing extra hypotheses.
AI.motivation: Previous attempts to describe relaxation to thermodynamic equilibrium using classical (Hamilton's equations) or quantum (Schrödinger equation) approaches have failed without additional hypotheses. The authors aim to demonstrate that equilibrium can be reached naturally by imposing uncertainty principle-based boundary conditions.
AI.method: The authors impose non-strict boundary conditions on a classical gaseous system, where all interactions with container walls follow Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, rather than deterministic reflection laws.
AI.result: The system successfully reaches thermodynamic equilibrium states through this approach, without requiring any supplementary assumptions beyond the uncertainty principle at the boundaries.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating quantum uncertainty at the boundaries of a classical system provides a sufficient mechanism for relaxation to thermodynamic equilibrium, bridging classical and quantum descriptions of irreversibility.

title: Energy-Weighted Site Percolation in Two Dimensions
summary: We study a generalization of two-dimensional site percolation by assigning an energy cost $\varepsilon$ to bonds between nearest-neighbor occupied sites. This leads to a competition between entropy-driven cluster growth and energetic suppression (or enhancement) of connectivity. Varying $\varepsilon$ continuously interpolates between dense ferromagnetic-like clusters, ordinary classical percolation, and a dilute regime of minimally connected isolated clusters. Using Monte Carlo simulations and real-space renormalization-group (RG) methods, we show that bond energy shifts the percolation threshold smoothly. We define an energy-weighted correlation length that remains finite at the classical site occupation threshold ($p_c(\varepsilon=0)$) and shrinks with increasing $\varepsilon$, capturing the energetic suppression of large-scale connectivity. The cluster size distribution exhibits an energy-dependent cutoff that drives the transition from percolation-like clusters to isolated clusters. A real-space RG with Kadanoff block recursions reveals a systematic evolution of the correlation-length exponent $ν$ from $ν=1/2$ (dense clusters) to $ν=4/3$ (classical percolation), approaching $ν=1$ (minimally connected isolated clusters), in agreement with Coulomb-gas predictions for loop models where bond energy renormalizes loop fugacity. For large values of \(\varepsilon\) (isotropic case), the suppression of nearest-neighbor bonds results in the emergence of antiferromagnetic sub-lattice ordering at high densities. Additionally, anisotropic bond energies lead to directionally selective cluster growth. Finally, we also discuss a lattice gas RG approach and scenarios where bond energy is renormalized across different scales.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates a generalized 2D site percolation model with bond energy costs, showing via Monte Carlo and RG methods that varying energy ε smoothly shifts the percolation threshold, modifies correlation length and cluster size distributions, and changes critical exponents from ν=1/2 (dense) to ν=4/3 (classical) to ν=1 (isolated clusters), with emergent antiferromagnetic ordering at high ε and anisotropic bond energies enabling directional cluster growth.
AI.motivation: To understand the competition between entropy-driven cluster growth and energetic suppression/enhancement of connectivity in a generalized percolation model, and to explore how varying bond energy interpolates between different percolation regimes.
AI.method: Monte Carlo simulations combined with real-space renormalization-group (RG) methods, including Kadanoff block recursions and lattice gas RG, applied to a 2D site percolation model with bond energy cost ε.
AI.result: Bond energy smoothly shifts the percolation threshold; an energy-weighted correlation length remains finite at the classical threshold and shrinks with ε; the cluster size distribution has an energy-dependent cutoff; the correlation-length exponent ν evolves from 1/2 (dense) → 4/3 (classical) → 1 (isolated clusters), matching Coulomb-gas predictions; large ε induces antiferromagnetic sublattice ordering; anisotropic energies produce directionally selective growth.
AI.conclusion: The generalized percolation model with bond energy provides a continuous interpolation between dense, classical, and dilute percolation regimes, with renormalization of loop fugacity governing the critical behavior; the framework can be extended to anisotropic cases and lattice gas representations.

title: Simulating Exciton Transport with Complex Absorbing Potentials
summary: We introduce a stochastic framework based on complex absorbing potentials (CAPs) to investigate exciton transport in large molecular aggregates. Within this approach, CAPs act as non-Hermitian reservoirs and sinks that enable effective measurement of transport efficiency. We apply this framework to cyanine dye aggregates and examine how vacancy defects and system size influence exciton dynamics in two-dimensional sheets and quasi-one-dimensional tubes. We also introduce a CAPs-based classification scheme that links molecular packing in 2D aggregates to transport behavior. Our results demonstrate how aggregate topology and structural disorder govern exciton dynamics and provide guidance for designing materials with enhanced energy transport.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a stochastic framework using complex absorbing potentials (CAPs) to study exciton transport in molecular aggregates, applied to cyanine dye aggregates with vacancy defects and varying system sizes, and proposes a CAPs-based classification linking molecular packing to transport behavior.
AI.motivation: To develop a framework that effectively measures exciton transport efficiency in large molecular aggregates, addressing the challenge of understanding how aggregate topology and structural disorder govern exciton dynamics.
AI.method: A stochastic framework based on complex absorbing potentials (CAPs) acting as non-Hermitian reservoirs and sinks to measure transport efficiency, applied to cyanine dye aggregates in 2D sheets and quasi-1D tubes.
AI.result: Demonstrated how vacancy defects and system size influence exciton transport; introduced a CAPs-based classification scheme linking molecular packing in 2D aggregates to transport behavior.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate topology and structural disorder govern exciton dynamics; the framework provides guidance for designing materials with enhanced energy transport.

title: Simulation of S-parameters of general multilayer boxed PCBs with the method of moments and the scattering matrix algorithm
summary: Printed circuit board (PCB) modelling is an important part of the PCB production process, in which the designer aims to optimize the desired output characteristics prior to physical PCB manufacturing. Due to the specific shape of PCBs, namely, thin and highly conductive components enclosed within a relatively simply shaped dielectric host, the PCB modelling problem is amenable to solution by the so-called 2.5D Method of Moments (MoM) applied to the integral equation solution of Maxwell's equations. For this purpose, an analytic expression for the Green's function of the host medium needs to be derived. Many studies exist in which expressions are derived for the transverse Green's function components in a waveguide, used for modelling planar metallization layers in shielded layered media. Works containing the full Green's function that allows modelling of both longitudinal and transverse currents are much fewer. In this study, we propose a tool to solve the shielded PCB modelling problem involving both transverse and longitudinal currents, with the Green's function in a layered waveguide derived using the S-matrix formalism. Our approach combines a straightforward, intuitive way of calculating the complete dyadic Green's function in a layered waveguide with the inherent numerical stability of the S-matrix method. The Green's function is expressed in terms of three sets of S-matrices associated with the PCB layers in which the electric current source and the electric field observation point are located. The MoM is implemented using surface rooftop, volume pulse, and linear basis functions, for which we provide the overlap integrals, to model planar metallization layers and wire-like vertical interconnects. The validity of the method is demonstrated on two numerical examples. The method can be extended to other bases to model objects of various shapes.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a 2.5D Method of Moments (MoM) tool for shielded PCB modelling that handles both transverse and longitudinal currents, using a complete dyadic Green's function derived via the S-matrix formalism in layered waveguides, with numerical validation on two examples.
AI.motivation: PCB modelling is critical for optimizing output characteristics before physical manufacturing. Existing Green's function expressions for shielded layered media mostly address transverse components only; works providing the full dyadic Green's function for both transverse and longitudinal currents are scarce.
AI.method: The full dyadic Green's function in a layered waveguide is derived using the S-matrix formalism, expressed via three sets of S-matrices associated with PCB layers containing the source and observation points. The MoM is implemented using surface rooftop, volume pulse, and linear basis functions with provided overlap integrals.
AI.result: The method is validated on two numerical examples, demonstrating its capability to model both planar metallization layers and wire-like vertical interconnects. It is extensible to other basis functions for various object shapes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed tool provides a numerically stable, intuitive approach to shielded PCB modelling with complete dyadic Green's functions, addressing a gap in existing literature. The S-matrix-based formulation ensures stability, and the framework is generalizable.

title: Reprogrammable magnonic logic in a multiferroic heterostructure via magnetoelectric coupling
comment: 24 pages (main & supplemental) and 9 figures (4 main and 5 supplemental)
summary: The realization of fully reconfigurable, voltage-controlled, and programmable on-chip magnonic devices is essential to fully harness the potential of spin waves for signal processing, logic and neuromorphic computing. Yet, existing demonstrations of electrical tuning of magnonic responses are either volatile, current-driven and thus energy-inefficient, or rely on local strain modification limiting their scalability for wafer-scale integration. Here, we address this challenge using a BiFeO3/La0.67Sr0.33MnO3 multiferroic thin film heterostructure. We show that ferroelectric domain engineering in BiFeO3 enables deterministic tuning of the magnon dispersion of La0.67Sr0.33MnO3, producing frequency shifts up to $\sim 150 MHz$ and allowing reconfigurable waveguiding. Micro-focused Brillouin light scattering directly images these effects, revealing electrically defined magnonic waveguides and spatially programmable dispersion. Compared to conventional approaches, this method provides non-volatile and reversible control. Furthermore, using an inverse-design simulation code, we demonstrate the capability of our platform to perform advanced magnonic functions such as frequency demultiplexing. Our results open a new avenue for using magnetoelectric heterostructures for magnonic logic, with further applicability to reservoir and neuromorphic computing and AI driven magnonic devices.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates non-volatile, voltage-controlled tuning of magnon dispersion in a BiFeO3/La0.67Sr0.33MnO3 multiferroic heterostructure via ferroelectric domain engineering, enabling reconfigurable magnonic waveguides, programmable dispersion, and advanced functions like frequency demultiplexing for magnonic logic and neuromorphic computing.
AI.motivation: Existing electrical tuning of magnonic responses is volatile, current-driven (energy-inefficient), or relies on local strain modification with limited scalability, hindering fully reconfigurable, voltage-controlled, and programmable on-chip magnonic devices for signal processing, logic, and neuromorphic computing.
AI.method: A BiFeO3/La0.67Sr0.33MnO3 multiferroic thin film heterostructure is used; ferroelectric domain engineering in BiFeO3 enables deterministic tuning of magnon dispersion in La0.67Sr0.33MnO3. Effects are imaged via micro-focused Brillouin light scattering, and an inverse-design simulation code demonstrates advanced functions.
AI.result: Frequency shifts up to ~150 MHz, reconfigurable waveguiding, electrically defined magnonic waveguides, spatially programmable dispersion, non-volatile and reversible control, and capability for frequency demultiplexing are demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: This magnetoelectric heterostructure approach opens a new avenue for magnonic logic, reservoir and neuromorphic computing, and AI-driven magnonic devices.

title: Supercurrent spin Hall effect enabled nanopillar Josephson diodes
summary: In the recent years it has been possible to achieve diode-like, non-reciprocal current-voltage response in Josephson junctions, despite the intrinsic symmetry of the Josephson effect itself. This is typically achieved by incorporating Rashba spin-orbit coupling into the Josephson junction as a strong inversion symmetry breaking component, and external magnetic field as a tuneable time-reversal symmetry breaking component. However, the efficiencies of the external field tuneable Josephson-diodes have remained limited to less than 10 \%, often measured below 100 mK temperature. In this work we take a new approach where non-reciprocity is induced by intrinsic SOC in a heavy metal Josephson barrier via the predicted supercurrent spin-Hall effect. By measuring a series of Nb-Pt-Nb nanopillar junctions we demonstrated field tuneable Josephson diode efficiencies as high as 17\%, measured above liquid Helium temperature. This was possible by the realization of a net non-equilibrium spin segregation in the Pt barrier, due to the supercurrent spin-Hall effect in the Pt barrier, analogous to the normal spin-Hall effect. As the direction of the induced spin moment is determined by the bias current, an external magnetic field causes the associated phases to add with opposite signs for opposite current directions, resulting in a nonreciprocal supercurrent across the junction.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a Josephson diode with up to 17% efficiency above liquid helium temperature by using a Nb-Pt-Nb nanopillar junction, where non-reciprocity is induced by the supercurrent spin-Hall effect in the Pt barrier, eliminating the need for Rashba SOC and achieving higher efficiency than previous sub-10% devices operating below 100 mK.
AI.motivation: Existing Josephson diodes suffer from limited efficiency (below 10%) and require extremely low temperatures (below 100 mK), motivating the need for a new approach to achieve higher efficiency non-reciprocal supercurrent at more practical temperatures.
AI.method: The authors fabricated Nb-Pt-Nb nanopillar junctions and leveraged the supercurrent spin-Hall effect in the heavy metal (Pt) barrier to create a net non-equilibrium spin segregation, where bias current direction determines the induced spin moment, and an external magnetic field causes opposite phase additions for opposite current directions, yielding non-reciprocal supercurrent.
AI.result: Field-tuneable Josephson diode efficiencies up to 17% were achieved, measured above liquid helium temperature (4.2 K), significantly surpassing the previous sub-10% efficiency limit of Rashba-based Josephson diodes operating below 100 mK.
AI.conclusion: The supercurrent spin-Hall effect in a heavy metal barrier provides a viable mechanism for achieving high-efficiency Josephson diodes at elevated temperatures, offering a new pathway for non-reciprocal supercurrent devices without relying on Rashba SOC and external magnetic fields as separate symmetry-breaking components.

title: Learning inelastic constitutive models from stress-strain data under hard thermodynamic constraints
summary:
Machine learning approaches informed by physics have offered new insights into the discovery of constitutive models from data, helping overcome some limitations of traditional constitutive modelling while reducing the cost of otherwise computationally intensive simulations. Yet, most existing approaches only partially enforce the requirements of physics and thermodynamics, leaving open questions about their consistency across a broad range of material behaviours and their ability to generalise robustly to unseen loading paths when only limited measurements are available.
  This work establishes a thermodynamics-constrained learning framework whose architecture embeds the principles of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, objectivity and stability as hard, scalable constraints to learn constitutive models from standard macroscopic data. Analytical benchmarks involving stress-strain loading paths demonstrate that the method learns thermodynamically consistent and robust constitutive models for a range of inelastic materials of increasing complexity. At inference, the resulting models generalise to more demanding, unobserved paths and can autonomously recover interpretable internal variables that capture path-dependent evolution. The framework is then applied to granular media, prototypical heterogeneous and history-dependent materials for which constitutive modelling remains challenging. Trained on numerically simulated experiments based on the discrete element method, the model discovers the underlying constitutive equations and predicts responses under cyclic loading, including the emergence of hysteresis absent from the training data, relying solely on macroscopic stress-strain histories. The findings indicate that enforcing non-equilibrium thermodynamics through hard constraints represents a principled route to robust, consistent, and scalable data-driven discovery of constitutive models.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a thermodynamics-constrained learning framework that embeds non-equilibrium thermodynamics, objectivity, and stability as hard constraints to discover constitutive models from macroscopic data. It demonstrates robust generalization to unseen loading paths and recovers interpretable internal variables, successfully applied to granular media where it predicts hysteresis under cyclic loading.
AI.motivation: Existing physics-informed machine learning approaches for constitutive modeling only partially enforce thermodynamic consistency, limiting their generalizability and reliability across diverse material behaviors, especially when data is scarce.
AI.method: A neural network architecture with hard constraints encoding non-equilibrium thermodynamics principles, objectivity, and stability, trained on standard macroscopic stress-strain data.
AI.result: The method learns thermodynamically consistent models that generalize to unseen loading paths, recovers interpretable internal variables, and predicts hysteresis in granular media under cyclic loading using only macroscopic stress-strain histories.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing non-equilibrium thermodynamics through hard constraints provides a principled, robust, and scalable approach for data-driven discovery of constitutive models.

title: Specific heat and susceptibility of S=1/2 antiferromagnets on square, triangular, and kagome lattices
summary: We study the temperature dependence of the thermodynamic properties of spin-1/2 antiferromagnets on two-dimensional lattices. Our analysis employs the sine-square deformation (SSD), in which a real-space envelope function is applied to the Hamiltonian so that the local energy scale is smoothly reduced to zero at the system boundaries. The quantum eigenstates of the SSD Hamiltonian exhibit bulk-like behavior near the system center, effectively mimicking the thermodynamic limit even in small finite-size calculations. Using these fictitious bulk states, we compute the energy density, specific heat, and magnetic susceptibility as functions of temperature. We find that both the triangular- and kagome-lattice antiferromagnets show either a shoulder or a pronounced double-peak structure in the low-temperature specific heat, whereas the kagome case particularly shows a strong enhancement of magnetic susceptibility down to the lowest temperature range. These direct comparisons, together with the square-lattice and one-dimensional cases, reveal that although both frustrated systems retain a substantial amount of entropy, the low-energy excitations below ~ 0.5J of the kagome lattice are predominantly governed by the magnetic excited states, whereas not much for the triangular lattice.

AI.tldr: The paper uses sine-square deformation (SSD) to study thermodynamic properties of spin-1/2 antiferromagnets on 2D lattices (triangular, kagome, square) and 1D chains. SSD creates bulk-like states in finite systems, allowing calculation of energy density, specific heat, and magnetic susceptibility vs temperature. Results show that frustrated systems (triangular, kagome) exhibit shoulder or double-peak specific heat structures, with kagome showing strong low-T magnetic susceptibility enhancement due to magnetic excited states below ~0.5J.
AI.motivation: To understand the temperature-dependent thermodynamic behavior of frustrated 2D quantum antiferromagnets, particularly the nature of low-energy excitations in triangular and kagome lattices, using a method (SSD) that efficiently mimics the thermodynamic limit.
AI.method: Sine-square deformation (SSD) is applied to the Hamiltonian, where a real-space envelope function smoothly reduces local energy scale to zero at boundaries. Quantum eigenstates of the SSD Hamiltonian exhibit bulk-like behavior near the system center, enabling extraction of thermodynamic quantities (energy density, specific heat, magnetic susceptibility) from small finite-size calculations.
AI.result: Both triangular- and kagome-lattice antiferromagnets show shoulder or pronounced double-peak structure in low-temperature specific heat. Kagome lattice exhibits strong enhancement of magnetic susceptibility persisting to the lowest temperatures. Comparisons indicate that while both frustrated systems retain substantial entropy, kagome's low-energy excitations below ~0.5J are predominantly magnetic, whereas triangular's are not.
AI.conclusion: The low-energy physics of frustrated 2D antiferromagnets differs qualitatively: kagome lattice excitations below ~0.5J are dominated by magnetic states, while triangular lattice excitations are not primarily magnetic despite both retaining significant entropy.

title: Thermodynamic and statistical properties of a multifractional modified dispersion relation via the grand-canonical ensemble
comment: 31 pages and 7 figures. Suggestions are welcome
summary: We study the thermodynamic and statistical properties of a gas governed by a multifractional modified dispersion relation of the form $ω^{2}=k^{2}+4E_{*}^{-1/2}k^{5/2}$, where $E_{*}$ sets the characteristic scale of the multifractional correction. Working within the grand-canonical ensemble, we derive the modified density of states, the grand potential, the partition function, and the main thermodynamic quantities for both bosonic and fermionic sectors. The deformation changes the available phase-space distribution and produces nonstandard thermal scalings controlled by the ratio $T/E_{*}$. In the infrared regime, the usual relativistic gas behavior is recovered with leading corrections proportional to powers of $(T/E_{*})^{1/2}$. In the ultraviolet regime, the density of states scales as $\varrho(ω)\propto ω^{7/5}$, corresponding to an effective density-of-states dimension $d_{\mathrm{eff}}=12/5$. As a consequence, the Stefan-Boltzmann law is deformed from $u\propto T^{4}$ to $u\propto E_{*}^{3/5}T^{17/5}$, while the equation-of-state parameter approaches $w=5/12$ instead of the standard radiation value $w=1/3$. We also analyze thermal stability, particle number and energy fluctuations, Bose-Einstein condensation, and the degenerate Fermi gas limit. The multifractional correction increases the critical temperature of a conserved bosonic gas and modifies the Fermi energy, pressure, sound speed, and low-temperature heat capacity of degenerate fermions.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the thermodynamics of a gas with a multifractional dispersion relation $ω^2 = k^2 + 4E_*^{-1/2} k^{5/2}$, deriving modified density of states, grand potential, and thermodynamic quantities for bosons and fermions. Key results include deformed Stefan-Boltzmann law ($u \propto E_*^{3/5} T^{17/5}$), effective dimension $d_{\mathrm{eff}} = 12/5$, and equation-of-state parameter $w = 5/12$, along with altered Bose-Einstein condensation and degenerate Fermi gas properties.
AI.motivation: To understand how multifractional corrections to the dispersion relation, motivated by quantum gravity or multifractional spacetimes, modify the statistical mechanics and thermodynamic behavior of relativistic gases.
AI.method: Working within the grand-canonical ensemble, the authors derive the density of states, grand potential, and partition function for both bosonic and fermionic gases governed by the multifractional dispersion relation, and compute thermodynamic quantities analytically in infrared and ultraviolet regimes.
AI.result: The density of states scales as $\varrho(\omega) \propto \omega^{7/5}$ (effective dimension $d_{\mathrm{eff}}=12/5$). Stefan-Boltzmann law becomes $u \propto E_*^{3/5} T^{17/5}$, equation-of-state parameter $w=5/12$ (vs. $1/3$ for standard radiation). Critical temperature for Bose-Einstein condensation increases; Fermi energy, pressure, sound speed, and low-temperature heat capacity of degenerate fermions are modified.
AI.conclusion: Multifractional corrections significantly alter the thermodynamic behavior of quantum gases, producing nonstandard scalings controlled by $T/E_*$, with observable consequences for early Universe cosmology and compact objects.

title: Structure of Molten FeCl2 and FeCl3
comment: 26 total pages, 11 main figures, 6 supplementary figures
summary: Molten iron chlorides are central to emerging energy technologies, including electrochemical iron production and redox flow batteries. Optimizing their electrochemical performance and transport properties requires atomic-scale structural understanding, yet detailed data for molten FeCl2 and its differences from FeCl3 remain scarce. Here, we determined the structures of molten FeCl2 and FeCl3 using High Energy X-ray diffraction (HEXRD), Empirical Potential Structure Refinement (EPSR), and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs). HEXRD measurements provided structure factors and total radial distribution functions (RDFs), which were quantitatively reproduced through EPSR refinement directly constrained by experimental data. MD simulations using MACE foundation and fine-tuned models reproduced experimental structure factors as well as total and partial RDFs, capturing key structural differences between the melts. The models resolved the octahedral to tetrahedral coordination transition of Fe upon melting in FeCl3 and predicted a similar transition in FeCl2. Analysis of MD trajectories quantified coordination environments, bridging Cl populations, bond-angle distributions, and connectivity patterns, revealing distinct degrees of polymerization and local geometry. Polymer chain statistics further showed that, contrary to prior reports, both liquids predominantly consist of extended chains containing six or more Fe centers rather than discrete Fe2Cl6 units. Finally, diffusion coefficients of the two melts calculated from the MACE-MD simulations were compared. Together, these results establish atomic-scale structural benchmarks for molten FeCl2 and FeCl3 and demonstrate the reliability of MACE-based MLIPs for predictive modeling of high-temperature molten salts, while providing practical guidance for MLIP development in complex ionic liquids.

AI.tldr: The structures of molten FeCl2 and FeCl3 were determined using HEXRD, EPSR, and MLIP-based MD simulations, revealing distinct coordination environments, polymerization states (extended chains rather than discrete Fe2Cl6 units), and diffusion coefficients, establishing atomic-scale benchmarks and validating MACE-based MLIPs for high-temperature molten salt modeling.
AI.motivation: Molten iron chlorides are critical for emerging energy technologies like electrochemical iron production and redox flow batteries, yet detailed atomic-scale structural data for molten FeCl2 and its differences from FeCl3 remain scarce, motivating the need for comprehensive structural characterization.
AI.method: Combined High Energy X-ray diffraction (HEXRD), Empirical Potential Structure Refinement (EPSR) directly constrained by experimental data, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using MACE-based machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) including foundation and fine-tuned models.
AI.result: Quantitative reproduction of experimental structure factors and RDFs was achieved; octahedral-to-tetrahedral coordination transition upon melting was resolved in FeCl3 and predicted in FeCl2; both melts consist predominantly of extended chains (≥6 Fe centers) rather than discrete Fe2Cl6 units; diffusion coefficients were compared.
AI.conclusion: Atomic-scale structural benchmarks for molten FeCl2 and FeCl3 were established; MACE-based MLIPs demonstrated high reliability for predictive modeling of high-temperature molten salts, providing practical guidance for MLIP development in complex ionic liquids.

title: Frustration from Localized Zhang-Rice States: A Unified Theory of Doping-Driven Magnetic Transitions in Cuprates
comment: 4.5 pages, 3 figs, SM will be updated later
summary: The microscopic mechanism by which doped holes disrupt the antiferromagnetic order is one of the fundamental questions in cuprates. In this work, we propose a unified microscopic theory in which doped holes form spatially localized Zhang-Rice singlets which actively mediate emergent spin exchange. Rather than acting as simple non-magnetic vacancies, these localized states introduce emergent next-nearest $J_2$ and third-nearest $J_3$ neighbor superexchanges. This dopant-induced exchange pathway generates significant magnetic frustration, naturally explaining the rapid collapse of the Néel AFM order and the emergence of a spin-glass phase on the hole-doped side. Our findings provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex doping-driven magnetic phase transitions and magnetic electron-hole asymmetry in lightly doped cuprates.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes that doped holes in cuprates form localized Zhang-Rice singlets that mediate emergent superexchange interactions (J₂, J₃), generating magnetic frustration that explains the collapse of Néel antiferromagnetic order and the spin-glass phase in lightly doped cuprates.
AI.motivation: To understand the microscopic mechanism by which doped holes disrupt antiferromagnetic order in cuprates, a fundamental open question in the field.
AI.method: A unified microscopic theory where doped holes form spatially localized Zhang-Rice singlets that actively mediate emergent spin exchange interactions (next-nearest J₂ and third-nearest J₃ superexchanges), rather than acting as simple non-magnetic vacancies.
AI.result: The dopant-induced exchange pathway generates significant magnetic frustration, naturally explaining the rapid collapse of Néel AFM order and the emergence of a spin-glass phase on the hole-doped side.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a comprehensive understanding of complex doping-driven magnetic phase transitions and magnetic electron-hole asymmetry in lightly doped cuprates.

title: Fast and accurate committor estimation for kinetics simulations
summary: Computing long-timescale kinetics of biomolecular processes remains a major challenge for atomistic simulations. A way out is to exploit local kinetic information to construct the global stationary flux across the reaction space. The committor serves as the optimal reaction coordinate for this purpose; however, its calculation is itself highly demanding. Here, we introduce a fast and accurate algorithm for committor estimation by leveraging highly parallelizable short trajectory simulations and analogue prediction. The resulting committor is represented via a neural network ansatz and subsequently coupled with the Milestoning method to predict the mean first passage time at very low computational cost. We demonstrate the robustness and efficiency of this committor-guided Milestoning (CoM) method through examples of increasing complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoM (committor-guided Milestoning), which combines short parallel trajectory simulations with neural network-based committor estimation to efficiently predict long-timescale kinetics of biomolecular processes at low computational cost.
AI.motivation: Computing long-timescale kinetics of biomolecular processes via atomistic simulations remains a major challenge, and the committor—while being the optimal reaction coordinate for this purpose—is itself highly demanding to compute.
AI.method: The algorithm leverages highly parallelizable short trajectory simulations and analogue prediction to estimate the committor, represents it via a neural network ansatz, and couples it with the Milestoning method to predict the mean first passage time.
AI.result: The committor-guided Milestoning (CoM) method demonstrates robustness and efficiency across examples of increasing complexity.
AI.conclusion: CoM provides a fast and accurate way to compute long-timescale kinetics by combining neural network-based committor estimation with Milestoning at very low computational cost.

title: Free-particle Green's function matrix elements over spherical Gaussian and plane-wave-modulated Gaussian basis functions
summary: Free-particle Green's function plays a central role in the theoretical description of electron scattering and autoionization processes in quantum physics and chemistry. Recently, Gaussian basis set approaches have become increasingly important in applications to unbound and metastable electronic states. However, the practical use of such methods has been limited by the lack of efficient and compact analytical expressions for matrix elements of the free-particle Green's function in Gaussian-based representations. Here we present a novel, general analytical framework for the evaluation of one- and two-center matrix elements of the free-particle Green's function over spherical Gaussian basis functions and plane-wave-modulated spherical Gaussians. The derivation is based on the Fourier transform of Gaussian functions together with the addition theorem of harmonic polynomials, leading to compact closed-form expressions and efficient recurrence relations. We also analyze the asymptotic behavior of the free-particle Green's function matrix elements, which is essential in the description of low-energy continuum electrons using finite Gaussian basis sets.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a new analytical framework for computing matrix elements of the free-particle Green's function using Gaussian basis sets, addressing a key limitation in modeling unbound and metastable electronic states.
AI.motivation: Gaussian basis set approaches are increasingly important for describing unbound and metastable electronic states (e.g., electron scattering, autoionization), but practical use has been limited by the lack of efficient, compact analytical expressions for free-particle Green's function matrix elements in such representations.
AI.method: The derivation employs the Fourier transform of Gaussian functions combined with the addition theorem of harmonic polynomials, yielding compact closed-form expressions and efficient recurrence relations for one- and two-center matrix elements over spherical Gaussian basis functions and plane-wave-modulated spherical Gaussians.
AI.result: Novel general analytical framework enabling efficient evaluation of matrix elements; analysis of asymptotic behavior crucial for describing low-energy continuum electrons using finite Gaussian basis sets.
AI.conclusion: The framework overcomes previous limitations, making Gaussian basis set methods practically viable for studying continuum and metastable electronic states with compact and efficient analytical expressions.

title: New Source of Spin-hot spot in displaced silicon double quantum dots
summary: Controlling electron spins in double quantum dots allows individual electrons to be trapped and manipulated for next-generation solid-state qubit devices. In this paper, the study analyzes spin relaxation due to deformation potentials of acoustic phonon in single and double quantum dots under in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields, showing that in single quantum dots the relaxation rate is highly sensitive to low in-plane magnetic fields ($<1T$) but converges near a spin-hot-spot region. In a single quantum dot, the spin-hot spot arises from well-understood level crossings between singlet and triplet states. In double quantum dots, a new and unusual spin-hot spot appears as the dots are pulled apart from the origin, with spin-relaxation rates three orders of magnitude lower than conventional single quantum dots.
