In displaced quantum dots dominated by magnetic confinement, two distinct spin-hot spots appear at different in-plane magnetic field strengths, where spin-relaxation time varies from millisecond to picosecond. When quantum dots are separated by about 60 nm, calculations predict oscillations in spin-hot spots as the in-plane magnetic field changes. These unusual spin-hot spot oscillations occur at low magnetic fields ($<1T$), resulting in spin-relaxation rates about four orders of magnitude lower than those of conventional high-field spin-hot spots ($\approx 4.5T$). The extremely low spin-relaxation rate at the spin-hot spot enables the preparation of qubit superposition states for quantum computing and information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes spin relaxation in single and double quantum dots due to acoustic phonon deformation potentials under magnetic fields. It identifies new spin-hot spot phenomena in displaced double quantum dots with relaxation rates orders of magnitude lower than conventional single quantum dots, enabling qubit superposition state preparation for quantum computing.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize spin relaxation mechanisms in quantum dots for developing next-generation solid-state qubit devices, particularly exploring how deformation potentials of acoustic phonons affect spin relaxation under various magnetic field configurations.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis of spin relaxation due to deformation potentials of acoustic phonons in single and double quantum dots under in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields, examining different dot configurations and separation distances.
AI.result: In single quantum dots, relaxation rate is highly sensitive to low in-plane magnetic fields (<1T) but converges near spin-hot spot regions arising from singlet-triplet level crossings. In double quantum dots, a new spin-hot spot emerges as dots are pulled apart, with relaxation rates three orders of magnitude lower. At ~60 nm separation, oscillations in spin-hot spots occur at low fields (<1T), yielding rates four orders of magnitude lower than conventional high-field spin-hot spots (~4.5T).
AI.conclusion: The extremely low spin-relaxation rates at spin-hot spots in double quantum dots enable preparation of qubit superposition states, advancing quantum computing and information processing applications.

title: Disorder effect on the superfluid density and the origin of the pseudogap end point in the cuprate superconductors
summary: A major puzzle in the study of the cuprate superconductivity is the origin of the pseudogap end point. Intriguingly, such a critical doping is also where the superfluid density of the system reaches its maximum. A non-monotonic doping dependence of the superfluid density is rather unusual since the Drude weight of the cuprate system is found to increase monotonically with the doping concentration. It is generally believed that such a peculiar behavior should be attributed to both the strongly correlated nature of the cuprate system and the disorder effect. In this work, we develop a variational theory for the zero temperature superfluid density of the disordered $t-J$ model. This is achieved in two steps. First, we perform an unrestricted variational optimization of an RVB variational ground state for the disordered $t-J$ model. Second, we construct the variational state that describes the paramagnetic current response on such an RVB state. The zero temperature superfluid density $ρ_{s}(0)$ is then extracted from the curvature of the variational ground state energy of the system as a function of the external electromagnetic field. We find that $ρ_{s}(0)$ computed in this way is remarkably robust against the disorder effect. More specifically, we find that $ρ_{s}(0)$ is a monotonically increasing function of doping concentration $x$ and scales linearly with the total optical weight. This is consistent with the observation in the underdoped cuprates but is strongly at odd with the behavior in the overdoped cuprates. The strong contrast between the disorder effect in the underdoped and the overdoped regime lends strong support to our previous proposal that there exist a Mott transition between a doped-Mott-insulating metal in the underdoped regime and a fermi-liquid-like metal in the overdoped regime around the pseudogap end point.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a variational theory for zero-temperature superfluid density in the disordered t-J model, finding that superfluid density increases monotonically with doping and is robust against disorder in underdoped cuprates but inconsistent with overdoped behavior, supporting a Mott transition near the pseudogap end point.
AI.motivation: To explain the origin of the pseudogap end point in cuprate superconductors, where superfluid density peaks non-monotonically with doping — a puzzle given the monotonic increase of Drude weight. The authors aim to understand whether disorder and strong correlations can account for this behavior.
AI.method: A variational theory is developed for the zero-temperature superfluid density of the disordered t-J model. First, an unrestricted variational optimization of an RVB (resonating valence bond) variational ground state is performed. Then, a variational state describing paramagnetic current response is constructed. Superfluid density is extracted from the curvature of the variational ground state energy as a function of external electromagnetic field.
AI.result: Superfluid density ρ_s(0) is remarkably robust against disorder, increases monotonically with doping x, and scales linearly with total optical weight. This matches underdoped cuprate observations but contradicts overdoped cuprate behavior.
AI.conclusion: The contrasting disorder effects between underdoped and overdoped regimes support the existence of a Mott transition from a doped-Mott-insulating metal (underdoped) to a Fermi-liquid-like metal (overdoped) around the pseudogap end point, explaining the non-monotonic superfluid density.

title: Interface engineering of the anomalous Hall effect in Ni-based heterostructures
summary: Using a combined experimental and first-principles theoretical approach, we demonstrate interface engineering of the anomalous Hall effect in Ni-based epitaxial thin-film heterostructures. Ferromagnetic Ni thin films are grown on (001)-oriented single-crystal LaAlO$_3$, SrTiO$_3$, and MgO substrates, which impose different biaxial tensile strains of 0.3%, 0.6%, and 0.8%, respectively. Our room-temperature Hall transport measurements reveal a pronounced substrate-dependent modulation of the anomalous Hall conductivity. Interestingly, our calculations show that strain alone cannot account for the experimentally observed trends. Instead, we identify interfacial inversion-symmetry breaking, which induces Rashba spin-orbit interaction, as the key mechanism governing the anomalous Hall conductivity across different interfaces. Building on this understanding, we further demonstrate both theoretically and experimentally that the anomalous Hall conductivity can be continuously tuned by an external electric field. These findings establish the critical role of substrate-induced interfacial effects in controlling the anomalous Hall effect in engineered heterostructures and provide a viable pathway toward electrically tunable room-temperature spintronic devices.

AI.tldr: Interface engineering of the anomalous Hall effect in Ni-based epitaxial thin-film heterostructures is demonstrated using experiments and first-principles calculations. Substrate-dependent modulation of anomalous Hall conductivity arises not from strain but from interfacial inversion-symmetry breaking inducing Rashba spin-orbit interaction. External electric field enables continuous tuning of the anomalous Hall conductivity, offering a pathway for electrically tunable room-temperature spintronic devices.
AI.motivation: To understand the mechanism governing the anomalous Hall effect in Ni-based epitaxial heterostructures and to achieve electrical tunability of the anomalous Hall conductivity for spintronic applications.
AI.method: Combined experimental measurements (room-temperature Hall transport on Ni thin films grown on LaAlO₃, SrTiO₃, and MgO substrates) and first-principles theoretical calculations; comparison of strain effects vs. interfacial inversion-symmetry breaking; electric field tuning experiments.
AI.result: Substrate-dependent modulation of anomalous Hall conductivity is observed. Strain alone cannot explain the trends; interfacial inversion-symmetry breaking inducing Rashba spin-orbit interaction is identified as the key mechanism. Anomalous Hall conductivity can be continuously tuned by an external electric field.
AI.conclusion: Substrate-induced interfacial effects critically control the anomalous Hall effect in engineered heterostructures, enabling electrically tunable room-temperature spintronic devices.

title: Partial Kondo Screening Solves the Mystery of Rare Earth Tetraborides
summary: We invoke a new mechanism to account for multiple magnetization plateaus observed in rare-earth tetraborides. Using a combination of hybrid and semiclassical Monte Carlo simulations of the Kondo lattice model (KLM) on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice (SSL), we find robust magnetization plateaus at fractions 1/6, 2/9, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3 and 3/4 of the saturation magnetization. We find that most of the plateau states are partially Kondo screened and emerge from the field-tuning of a complex three-way competition between the kinetic energy, the Kondo coupling, and the magnetic frustration. Most remarkably, the unusual magneto-transport reported in ErB$_4$ and TmB$_4$ admits an unexpectedly simple explanation within our mechanism. This work not only provides an elegant and simple solution to the long-standing puzzle of metamagnetism and anomalous magnetotransport in RB$_4$, but also introduces a novel mechanism to predict and discover new correlated phases in frustrated Kondo lattices.

AI.tldr: Using Monte Carlo simulations of the Kondo lattice model on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice, the authors discover robust magnetization plateaus at fractions 1/6, 2/9, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, and 3/4 of saturation, attributed to a three-way competition between kinetic energy, Kondo coupling, and magnetic frustration, offering a simple explanation for anomalous magnetotransport in rare-earth tetraborides like ErB₄ and TmB₄.
AI.motivation: To resolve the long-standing puzzle of multiple magnetization plateaus and anomalous magnetotransport observed in rare-earth tetraborides (RB₄), which existing mechanisms failed to adequately explain.
AI.method: Hybrid and semiclassical Monte Carlo simulations of the Kondo lattice model (KLM) on the Shastry-Sutherland lattice (SSL).
AI.result: Robust magnetization plateaus at fractions 1/6, 2/9, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, and 3/4 of saturation magnetization; most plateau states are partially Kondo screened and arise from field-tuning of kinetic energy, Kondo coupling, and magnetic frustration.
AI.conclusion: Provides an elegant and simple solution to metamagnetism and anomalous magnetotransport in RB₄, and introduces a novel mechanism for predicting correlated phases in frustrated Kondo lattices.

title: From bulk to interface dynamics, in and out of equilibrium
summary: We study the dynamics of weakly deformed interfaces separating two stable phases, starting from the fluctuating hydrodynamics of the phase-separating fields. Using a well-chosen definition for the interface and the dynamical-action formalism to represent path probabilities, we derive the linear relaxation of the interface and the fluctuations around it for a large class of models. Our method applies to equilibrium dynamics, where it recovers and complements existing results, but also extends to their non-equilibrium counterparts. We explain how non-linear terms can be systematically computed and illustrate their derivations in the case of (active) model A. We highlight the danger of a popular ansatz used to derive interface dynamics, which was rigorously established in equilibrium but is uncontrolled for active field theories.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the linear relaxation and fluctuations of weakly deformed interfaces in phase-separating systems using fluctuating hydrodynamics and dynamical-action formalism, applicable to both equilibrium and non-equilibrium dynamics. It also warns about the uncontrolled nature of a popular ansatz for active field theories.
AI.motivation: To develop a general framework for understanding interface dynamics in phase-separating systems that works for both equilibrium and non-equilibrium settings, and to address the limitations of existing approaches.
AI.method: The authors use fluctuating hydrodynamics of phase-separating fields with a carefully defined interface, employ the dynamical-action formalism to represent path probabilities, and derive linear relaxation and fluctuations. Non-linear terms are computed systematically, illustrated for (active) model A.
AI.result: The method recovers and complements existing equilibrium results and extends to non-equilibrium systems. It reveals that a popular ansatz for deriving interface dynamics, rigorously valid in equilibrium, is uncontrolled for active field theories.
AI.conclusion: A systematic derivation of interface dynamics from fluctuating hydrodynamics is possible for a broad class of models, but caution is needed when applying equilibrium-based approximations to active matter systems.

title: Real-time Multi-instrument Autonomous Discovery of Novel Phase-change Memory Materials
summary: Autonomous labs enable the integration of automated experiment execution, data analysis and decision making. The main challenge remains the integration of diverse data streams from multiple instruments, where the data is often heterogeneous and unsynchronized. The standard learning process of undetermined synthesis-process-structure-property relationships (SPSPR) usually relies on post-experiment analysis after data is fully collected, not during live experiments, and decision making is carried out independently across characterization equipment. Here, we demonstrate the Multi-instrument Autonomous Discovery (MAD) framework -- combining structural property mapping and functional property optimization simultaneously in a closed-loop manner. As an example, we applied MAD to phase change memory (PCM) materials, and, in particular on the Mn-Sb-Te ternary, a previously unexplored materials system for PCM. A multi-output model is employed to merge data from x-ray diffraction (XRD) and electrical resistance measurements simultaneously through a co-regionalization kernel that models the relationship between them. The output probabilistic posterior and uncertainty quantification facilitate decision making with shared knowledge, while the goals are different across tasks. We aimed to maximize the knowledge of crystal structure distribution using non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), while in parallel, we find the composition with the maximum resistance value, an important figure of merit for PCM. Leveraging MAD, we found promising electrical PCMs and identified the SPSPR within 25 closed-loop iterations, corresponding to a seven-fold speed-up. The framework opens a new path of study in large-scale autonomous facilities, where future experiments can be run in parallel together, not independently.

AI.tldr: The paper presents MAD (Multi-instrument Autonomous Discovery), a closed-loop framework that integrates structural (XRD) and functional (electrical resistance) measurements simultaneously using multi-output co-regionalization models, enabling autonomous discovery of phase change memory materials with a seven-fold speed-up compared to traditional sequential approaches.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous labs struggle with integrating heterogeneous, unsynchronized data streams from multiple instruments. Standard learning of synthesis-process-structure-property relationships relies on post-experiment analysis rather than live decision-making, and characterization equipment operates independently rather than collaboratively.
AI.method: MAD framework combines structural property mapping (XRD) and functional property optimization (electrical resistance) in a closed-loop manner. A multi-output model with a co-regionalization kernel merges data from both instruments. Structural knowledge is maximized via non-negative matrix factorization (NMF), while functional optimization targets maximum resistance values. Bayesian posterior and uncertainty quantification guide shared decision-making across tasks.
AI.result: Applied to Mn-Sb-Te ternary system (previously unexplored for PCM), MAD discovered promising electrical PCM compositions and identified synthesis-process-structure-property relationships within 25 closed-loop iterations, achieving a seven-fold speed-up over traditional methods.
AI.conclusion: The MAD framework enables parallel, synchronized multi-instrument autonomous experimentation, opening new pathways for large-scale autonomous facilities where future experiments can run concurrently rather than independently.

title: Low-energy electron attachment to $\text{NO}_2$: absolute cross sections
comment: 18 pages, 2 figures and 2 tables. This manuscript has been submitted to Chemical Physics Letters
summary:
Resonances from electron attachment to $\text{NO}_2$ have been identified in the total electron scattering cross sections (TCS) measured with a magnetically confined electron transmission apparatus. The corresponding absolute electron attachment cross sections have been derived from the TCS values through a self-consistent scattering channel deconvolution process. The positions of some of these resonances are consistent with previous elastic scattering calculations and dissociative electron attachment experiments. However, both the observed positions and the magnitude of the present resonance cross sections are in contradiction with the available recommended TCS values thus suggesting that electron scattering cross section databases need to be updated.
  Keywords: electron scattering resonances, negative ion formation, electron attachment cross sections

AI.tldr: This paper identifies resonances from electron attachment to NO₂ using total electron scattering cross sections (TCS) measured with a magnetically confined electron transmission apparatus. Absolute electron attachment cross sections are derived via self-consistent deconvolution. The findings contradict existing recommended TCS values, suggesting outdated databases require updating.
AI.motivation: To identify resonances from electron attachment to NO₂ and derive accurate absolute cross sections, while addressing discrepancies with existing recommended TCS values that suggest databases need updating.
AI.method: Total electron scattering cross sections (TCS) were measured using a magnetically confined electron transmission apparatus. A self-consistent scattering channel deconvolution process was applied to derive absolute electron attachment cross sections from the TCS values.
AI.result: Some resonance positions align with previous elastic scattering calculations and dissociative electron attachment experiments. However, both the positions and magnitudes of the resonance cross sections contradict the available recommended TCS values.
AI.conclusion: Current electron scattering cross section databases are inaccurate and need updating based on the newly measured and derived cross section data for NO₂.

title: Electronic mechanism of sub-100-fs demagnetization induced by a femtosecond light pulse
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 85 references; includes Supplementary Information (1 pdf file - 8 pages, 6 figures). This is the author created version of an article accepted for publication in Scientific Reports journal. The article has been published on a gold open access basis under a CC BY 4.0 licence
summary: A quantitative understanding of the processes that trigger light-induced demagnetization on ultrashort timescales is crucial for achieving an ultrafast, radiation-controlled magnetic response in materials. This milestone is essential for developing next-generation magnetic storage devices and ultrafast magnetic switches. In this theoretical study, we investigated demagnetization triggered in a single magnetic domain by light pulses ranging from a few to a few tens of femtoseconds in duration, with photon energies spanning the optical and X-ray regimes, under strongly non-equilibrium conditions. We predicted a loss of magnetization in the sub-100-fs range in all cases, primarily due to the excitation of the electronic system and the subsequent redistribution of electrons within the magneto-sensitive band. The considered timescales were too short for phonon-mediated processes or inter-site Heisenberg exchange processes to contribute significantly. These findings pave the way for highly accurate, radiation-driven magnetization control in magnetic materials at sub-100-femtosecond timescales with potential practical applications.

AI.tldr: This theoretical study investigates light-induced demagnetization in a single magnetic domain on sub-100-femtosecond timescales using ultrashort light pulses (few to tens of femtoseconds) across optical to X-ray photon energies. The predicted magnetization loss is primarily due to electronic excitation and redistribution within magneto-sensitive bands, with negligible contributions from phonon or Heisenberg exchange processes on these timescales.
AI.motivation: To achieve ultrafast, radiation-controlled magnetic response in materials for next-generation magnetic storage devices and ultrafast magnetic switches by quantitatively understanding light-induced demagnetization on ultrashort timescales.
AI.method: Theoretical investigation of demagnetization in a single magnetic domain triggered by light pulses of varying durations (few to tens of femtoseconds) and photon energies (optical to X-ray) under strongly non-equilibrium conditions.
AI.result: Predicted magnetization loss in sub-100-fs range in all cases, primarily due to electronic excitation and subsequent electron redistribution within the magneto-sensitive band, with no significant contribution from phonon-mediated or inter-site Heisenberg exchange processes.
AI.conclusion: These findings enable highly accurate, radiation-driven magnetization control in magnetic materials at sub-100-femtosecond timescales with potential practical applications in ultrafast magnetic devices.

title: Observation of a Mott quantum spin Hall insulator in twisted WSe2
summary: Quantum spin Hall (QSH) insulators and Mott insulators are conventionally regarded as distinct insulating phases, arising from band topology and strong Coulomb interactions, respectively. Here, we report the observation of QSH edge transport in a magnetic-field-stabilized Mott insulating state at half filling of the second moire band in a 2.29 degree twisted WSe2 device. This state exhibits a resistance plateau identical to that of the single-particle QSH state at full filling of the first moire valence band, indicating the same number of helical edge channels. Electrical transport measurements reveal nearly quantized resistance that is insensitive to vertical electric field, out-of-plane magnetic field, and temperature below 5 K. Pronounced nonlocal transport and strong negative in-plane magnetoconductance further support helical edge conduction, establishing robust edge transport in the strongly correlated regime. Temperature-dependent Hall measurements reveal a characteristic temperature scale of approximately 10 K, corresponding to an energy scale of about 1 meV. Our results demonstrate that spin-conserved QSH edge states can persist in a half filled, strongly correlated insulating phase and under external magnetic field, opening a route toward interaction-resilient topological transport in moire quantum materials.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the observation of quantum spin Hall (QSH) edge transport in a magnetic-field-stabilized Mott insulating state at half filling of the second moire band in twisted WSe2, demonstrating that topological edge states can persist in strongly correlated insulating phases.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether QSH edge states can survive in strongly correlated regimes (Mott insulators), where conventional band topology and strong Coulomb interactions are typically considered mutually exclusive.
AI.method: Electrical transport measurements on a 2.29-degree twisted WSe2 device at half filling of the second moire band, including resistance plateau analysis, nonlocal transport, magnetoconductance, and temperature-dependent Hall measurements.
AI.result: A resistance plateau identical to the single-particle QSH state, nearly quantized resistance insensitive to electric field, out-of-plane magnetic field, and temperature below 5 K; pronounced nonlocal transport and strong negative in-plane magnetoconductance; characteristic temperature scale ~10 K (energy scale ~1 meV).
AI.conclusion: Spin-conserved QSH edge states can persist in a half-filled, strongly correlated Mott insulating phase and under external magnetic field, opening a route toward interaction-resilient topological transport in moire quantum materials.

title: Enhancement of superconductivity by polarization of magnetic impurities in disordered films
summary: Dirty superconducting films with magnetic impurities can exhibit nontrivial behavior in a magnetic field that polarizes the impurity spins. As predicted by Kharitonov and Feigelman (KF) [JETP Lett. 82, 421 (2005)], this polarization reduces the exchange scattering rate. Consequently, a parallel magnetic field can enhance the critical temperature $T_c$ when magnetic-field pair breaking is weak, as realized for strong spin-orbit scattering and small film thickness. Recently, Llanos et al. [Nat. Phys. (2026)] observed a pronounced enhancement of $T_c$ consistent with the KF theory. The same experiment also reported an enhancement of the perpendicular upper critical field $H_{c2}^{\perp}$ and a suppression of the London penetration depth $λ_L$ by a parallel magnetic field. These quantities were not considered in the original KF theory. To address this gap, we develop a theoretical framework based on Gor'kov's diagrammatic technique for dirty superconductors. We extend the KF theory in two experimentally relevant directions: (i) to arbitrary temperatures $T<T_c$ and several superconducting observables, and (ii) to arbitrary magnetic-field orientations. As a result, we demonstrate theoretically the suppression of $λ_L$ and the enhancement of $H_{c2}^{\perp}$ by a parallel magnetic field, in agreement with experiment.

AI.tldr: The authors extend Kharitonov-Feigelman theory to explain how a parallel magnetic field enhances the perpendicular upper critical field and suppresses London penetration depth in dirty superconducting films with magnetic impurities, matching recent experimental observations.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments observed enhancement of perpendicular upper critical field H_{c2}^{\perp} and suppression of London penetration depth λ_L by a parallel magnetic field, which were not addressed in the original Kharitonov-Feigelman theory. This work aims to fill that theoretical gap.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical framework using Gor'kov's diagrammatic technique for dirty superconductors, extending the KF theory to arbitrary temperatures below T_c and various superconducting observables, as well as to arbitrary magnetic-field orientations.
AI.result: The theory demonstrates theoretically that a parallel magnetic field suppresses λ_L and enhances H_{c2}^{\perp}, consistent with experimental findings by Llanos et al.
AI.conclusion: The extended KF theory successfully explains the experimentally observed nontrivial magnetic field effects on multiple superconducting properties beyond just T_c enhancement.

title: An Efficient Approach for Calculating Free Energy in Molecular Dynamics: Demineralization of Hydroxyapatite as a Case Study
summary: Despite the strength of Molecular Dynamics simulations in providing insights into the microscopic details of phenomenon in many fields in materials science, physics and biology, the biggest barrier is its limited timescale which is several orders of magnitude lower than the timescale of the real-world processes and phenomena being modeled. Free energy calculations are designed as a remedy to this problem that in theory can overcome this barrier. This is particularly relevant for biomineralisation processes such as tooth mineral formation and dissolution, while reflecting a broader challenge in accurately modelling rare events and long-timescale phenomena across complex molecular systems. However, due to the novelty of the field, a number of questions remain outstanding pertaining to the best practice of applying this method. The non-equilibrium work approach based on the Jarzynski equation is one of the most promising free energy calculation methods. However, the biggest challenge for the broader use of this method is the question of how many simulations are required for an accurate free energy estimation. Comparing the free energy results with very long reversible pulling simulations of atom clusters from the surface, each taking 75 days on the 48-core Intel Xeon Platinum 8268 CPUs, in this study we showed that this question is irrelevant and higher quality and better equilibrated initial structures is the proper approach than simply based on the number of simulations. We designed a new adaptive free energy calculation methodology which combines high quality, high computational cost free energy values with lower quality, lower cost values to build up the entire free energy profile. In the best case scenario this method lowers manifold the computational cost required for the non-equilibrium work free energy calculations compared to both the regular method and the reversible simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a new adaptive free energy calculation methodology for Molecular Dynamics simulations that reduces computational cost by using high-quality, high-cost calculations combined with lower-quality, lower-cost ones, demonstrating that initial structure quality matters more than simulation quantity for accurate free energy estimation.
AI.motivation: Molecular Dynamics simulations suffer from limited timescales orders of magnitude below real-world processes. Free energy calculations can overcome this barrier, particularly for biomineralisation processes like tooth mineral formation/dissolution, but best practices remain unclear, especially regarding how many simulations are needed for accurate estimation.
AI.method: The authors compared free energy results from very long reversible pulling simulations (75 days on 48-core Intel Xeon Platinum 8268 CPUs) with non-equilibrium work approaches based on the Jarzynski equation. They designed an adaptive methodology that combines high-quality, high-cost free energy values with lower-quality, lower-cost values to build the entire free energy profile.
AI.result: The study showed that the question of simulation quantity is irrelevant; higher quality and better equilibrated initial structures are more important. The best-case scenario of the adaptive method lowered computational cost manifold compared to both regular non-equilibrium work calculations and reversible simulations.
AI.conclusion: Focusing on the quality and equilibration of initial structures is more effective than simply increasing the number of simulations for accurate free energy estimation. The proposed adaptive methodology significantly reduces computational cost while maintaining accuracy.

title: Design Principles for Singlet Fission in Aza-BODIPY Dimers: Spacer-Controlled Electronic Structure and Energy Ordering
summary: In this work, we investigate the role of spacers in tuning singlet-fission (SF) activity in aza-BODIPY dimers using a diabatic electronic-structure framework. A series of nine spacer-linked dimers is analyzed employing high-level multireference methods to evaluate the energetics and couplings of the locally excited (LE), charge-transfer (CT), and multiexcitonic (ME) states. The introduction of spacers reduces excessive state mixing that was observed in C-C bonded aza-BODIPY dimers and promotes the emergence of more distinct ME states, while preserving the CT-mediated interactions required for efficient SF. Furthermore, the substitution pattern, degree of conjugation, and introduction of acetylene units strongly modulate the relative state energetics and effective couplings, thereby tuning the SF rate over several orders of magnitude. These findings establish clear structure--property relationships and provide molecular design guidelines for optimizing SF activity in aza-BODIPY-based chromophores.

AI.tldr: This study uses high-level multireference methods to analyze how spacers tune singlet-fission activity in aza-BODIPY dimers, finding that spacers reduce excessive state mixing, promote distinct multiexcitonic states, and modulate SF rates over orders of magnitude through substitution patterns and conjugation, establishing structure-property guidelines for SF optimization.
AI.motivation: To understand how spacers can tune singlet-fission (SF) activity in aza-BODIPY dimers and establish structure-property relationships for optimizing SF efficiency, addressing the issue of excessive state mixing observed in directly C-C bonded dimers.
AI.method: A diabatic electronic-structure framework with high-level multireference methods was employed to analyze nine spacer-linked aza-BODIPY dimers, evaluating energetics and couplings of locally excited (LE), charge-transfer (CT), and multiexcitonic (ME) states.
AI.result: Spacers reduce excessive state mixing, promote distinct ME states while preserving CT-mediated interactions; substitution pattern, conjugation degree, and acetylene units modulate state energetics and couplings, tuning SF rates over several orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: Clear structure-property relationships are established, providing molecular design guidelines for optimizing SF activity in aza-BODIPY-based chromophores through rational spacer engineering.

title: Durable Enhancement of $\mathbf{MoS_2}$ Single-Layer Photoluminescence by Ultraviolet Laser Treatment Under Ambient Conditions
summary: Single-layer molybdenum disulfide ($MoS_2$) possesses significant potential for nanoscale optoelectronics, but achieving high-intensity, long-term-stable photoluminescence (PL) emission remains a challenge. In this work, we demonstrate a remarkably robust, more than 8-fold maximum enhancement in the PL intensity of exfoliated and CVD-grown single-layer $MoS_2$ via a non-destructive ultraviolet (UV) laser treatment method. This substantial increase in radiative efficiency is accompanied by a trion-to-neutral exciton transition in the PL signal and a corresponding blue shift of the Raman $E_{2g}^1$ and $A_{1g}$ vibrational modes, signaling successful electron depletion (p-doping) and formation of Mo-O bonds, respectively. Furthermore, we demonstrate precise spatial control over PL properties by confining PL treatment exclusively to the UV laser-treated area. Crucially, the enhanced PL performance shows exceptional longevity; the CVD sample and the exfoliated sample remained stable for the entire monitoring period (72 and 32 days, respectively) under ambient conditions. We further investigated UV laser treatment in a controlled-environment chamber under argon, nitrogen, and oxygen atmospheres, distinguishing the influence of oxygen as the PL treatment agent. These findings establish a reliable pathway for the permanent treatment of single-layer $MoS_2$ PL properties, an essential step toward practical, high-performance nanophotonic devices.

AI.tldr: A non-destructive UV laser treatment method enhances photoluminescence intensity of single-layer MoS₂ by over 8-fold, induces trion-to-exciton transition and p-doping, enables spatial control, and achieves long-term stability under ambient conditions for up to 72 days.
AI.motivation: Single-layer MoS₂ has great potential for nanoscale optoelectronics but suffers from insufficient photoluminescence intensity and long-term stability, hindering practical device applications.
AI.method: Non-destructive UV laser treatment was applied to exfoliated and CVD-grown single-layer MoS₂. PL and Raman spectroscopy characterized the optical changes. Controlled-environment experiments (Ar, N₂, O₂) isolated oxygen's role as the active treatment agent.
AI.result: Over 8-fold PL enhancement, trion-to-exciton transition, blue-shifted Raman modes (E₂g¹ and A₁g), spatial confinement of treatment, and stability for 72 days (CVD) and 32 days (exfoliated) under ambient conditions.
AI.conclusion: UV laser treatment provides a reliable, permanent pathway for engineering PL properties of single-layer MoS₂, enabling high-performance nanophotonic devices.

title: Enhanced $s^\pm$-wave superconductivity in electron-doped La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$
summary: In cuprates, electron doping yields a much lower superconducting $T_c$ than hole doping. For recently discovered nickelate superconductors, the analogous doping strategies become more challenging. Consequently, while hole-doped Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates have been extensively studied, electron-doped RP nickelates remain rarely explored both experimentally and theoretically. Here we fill this gap by systematically investigating the two-orbital bilayer model for three representative systems: bulk La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$ at ambient pressure and 15\,GPa, and a heterostructure La$_3$Ni$_2$O$_7$:La$_3$Al$_2$O$_7$ that provides a feasible experimental route to electron doping. Using first-principle calculations and large-scale dynamical cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations, we find that electron doping generically enhances $s^\pm$-wave pairing superconductivity (SC) in all three cases, with the heterostructure showing the highest $T_c$ in the underdoped regime. Furthermore, our results suggest an inter-orbital cooperative mechanism that the pairing on the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital, induced by that on the $d_{z^2}$ orbital, plays vital role in the SC. This work provides the first theoretical prediction of enhanced SC in electron-doped RP nickelates and calls for future experimental verification.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically predicts that electron doping in Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates enhances s±-wave pairing superconductivity, contrary to the trend in cuprates, with heterostructure La₃Ni₂O₇:La₃Al₂O₇ showing the highest Tc in the underdoped regime via an inter-orbital cooperative mechanism.
AI.motivation: Electron-doped RP nickelates are rarely explored despite extensive study of hole-doped counterparts, and the authors aim to fill this gap by systematically investigating electron doping effects on superconductivity in these systems.
AI.method: First-principle calculations combined with large-scale dynamical cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations applied to a two-orbital bilayer model for three systems: bulk La₃Ni₂O₇ at ambient pressure and 15 GPa, and a heterostructure La₃Ni₂O₇:La₃Al₂O₇.
AI.result: Electron doping generically enhances s±-wave pairing superconductivity in all three cases. The heterostructure exhibits the highest Tc in the underdoped regime. An inter-orbital cooperative mechanism is identified where d_{x^2-y^2} orbital pairing is induced by d_{z^2} orbital pairing, playing a vital role in superconductivity.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first theoretical prediction of enhanced superconductivity in electron-doped RP nickelates, calling for future experimental verification.

title: First-principles calculations of electrical conductivities of edge-modified graphene nanoribbons: strain effect
summary: We investigate the influence of strain on the electrical properties of graphene nanoribbons that have potential applications in making sensors and other optoelectronic devices. In particular, we chose pristine armchair graphene nanoribbons with 7 zigzag edges (7aGNRsH), boron doped armchair graphene nanoribbons with 7 zigzag edges (7aGNRsH-B) and armchair graphene nanoribbons with 7 zigzag edges that have one carbon atom vacancy (7aGNRsH-V). Based on first-principles calculations, results show that pristine unstrained 7aGNRsH is electrically nonconductive but turns to be electrically conductive in a wide range of energy spectrum, e.g., from IR to visible to UV, due to the application of strain engineering. In metallic unstrained and strained 7aGNRsH-B and 7aGNRsH-V, non-vanishing electrical conductivity in the IR, visible and UV energy spectrum regimes are observed. We also investigate the influence of strain on the Berry curvature of 7aGNRsH, 7aGNRsH-B and 7aGNRsH-V nanoribbons. The results show that fermions are spread through out the Brillion zone in the reciprocal space for semiconducting unstrained 7aGNRsH but localized near the $Γ$-point for strained 7aGNRsH that have out-of-plane deformations due to strain engineering. For metallics 7aGNRsH-B and 7aGNRsH-V, Berry curvature plots show that fermions are localized far away from the $Γ$-point. In two atom boron doped p-type armchair graphene nanoribbons with 7 zigzag edges (7aGNRsH-2B), large peaks in electrical conductivity at IR energy spectrum regimes can be observed. These peaks of electrical conductivities in 7aGNRSH-2B may be detectable in experimentally synthesized structure in Reference, JACS 137, 8872 (2016).

AI.tldr: This study uses first-principles calculations to investigate how strain affects the electrical properties of pristine, boron-doped, and vacancy-defected 7-armchair graphene nanoribbons (7aGNRsH). Strain induces conductivity in semiconducting pristine nanoribbons across IR-to-UV ranges, while metallic doped/defected variants show conductivity regardless. Berry curvature analysis reveals strain-dependent fermion localization. Notably, doubly boron-doped 7aGNRsH-2B exhibits large IR conductivity peaks, potentially detectable experimentally.
AI.motivation: To understand how strain engineering can tune the electrical and optoelectronic properties of graphene nanoribbons for potential sensor and optoelectronic device applications.
AI.method: First-principles density functional theory (DFT) calculations on three types of 7-armchair graphene nanoribbons: pristine (7aGNRsH), boron-doped (7aGNRsH-B), and vacancy-defected (7aGNRsH-V), under applied strain. Berry curvature and electrical conductivity were computed.
AI.result: Pristine unstrained 7aGNRsH is nonconductive but becomes conductive (IR to UV) under strain. Metallic strained/unstrained 7aGNRsH-B and 7aGNRsH-V show finite conductivity across the spectrum. Berry curvature shows delocalized fermions in unstrained semiconductors, localized near Γ-point under strain, and far from Γ-point in metallic variants. 7aGNRsH-2B shows large IR conductivity peaks.
AI.conclusion: Strain engineering effectively modulates the electronic and transport properties of graphene nanoribbons, enabling tunable conductivity from IR to UV. The large IR peaks in 7aGNRsH-2B are of particular interest for experimental verification and device applications.

title: Graph-Theoretic Detection of Hilbert Space Fragmentation
summary: Hilbert-space fragmentation provides a mechanism for ergodicity breaking in quantum many-body systems even in the absence of disorder, leading to dynamically disconnected sectors and strong memory of initial conditions. However, identifying such structures is often challenging and typically relies on prior knowledge of conservation laws or model-specific analytical insight. Here we introduce an unbiased approach based on spectral graph theory and, within this framework, formulate the concept of nearly fragmented systems, in which perturbative processes couple otherwise fragmented sectors while preserving their dynamical imprint. By representing basis states as vertices and Hamiltonian matrix elements as edges, we map the connectivity structure of the many-body Hilbert space onto a graph and analyze it using tools such as the Laplacian spectrum, Fiedler vectors, and modularity. Exact fragmentation corresponds to disconnected graph components, while nearly fragmented systems manifest as weakly connected communities whose structure can still be resolved spectrally. Applying this framework to the one-dimensional $t$-$J$ model and its perturbations, we demonstrate that graph-theoretic diagnostics reliably identify both fragmented and nearly fragmented Hilbert-space structures and capture the hierarchy of dynamical time scales that governs the system's evolution. We further show that the method extends beyond kinetically constrained models by applying it directly to the Hubbard chain, where it reveals the emergence of nearly decoupled subspaces associated with doublon dynamics and spin configurations. Our results establish the spectral graph analysis as a general and scalable tool for diagnosing fragmentation and approximate dynamical constraints in complex quantum many-body systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an unbiased spectral graph theory approach to detect Hilbert-space fragmentation and near-fragmentation in quantum many-body systems, demonstrated on the t-J model and Hubbard chain.
AI.motivation: Identifying Hilbert-space fragmentation is challenging and typically relies on prior knowledge of conservation laws or model-specific insights; an unbiased, general approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors map basis states onto graph vertices and Hamiltonian matrix elements onto edges, then apply spectral graph theory tools (Laplacian spectrum, Fiedler vectors, modularity) to analyze connectivity. Exact fragmentation corresponds to disconnected components, while nearly fragmented systems appear as weakly connected communities resolvable spectrally.
AI.result: Applied to the 1D t-J model and its perturbations, graph-theoretic diagnostics reliably identify fragmented and nearly fragmented structures and capture the hierarchy of dynamical time scales. The method also reveals nearly decoupled subspaces (doublon dynamics and spin configurations) in the Hubbard chain.
AI.conclusion: Spectral graph analysis is established as a general, scalable tool for diagnosing Hilbert-space fragmentation and approximate dynamical constraints in complex quantum many-body systems.

title: Euler-Maruyama method for non-Wiener processes
summary: Descriptions of complex physical or biological systems often include stochastic contributions, and these are commonly simulated using Wiener processes. In many cases however, non-Gaussian fluctuations may originate from non-Wiener processes which remain less explored. The Euler-Maruyama method of discretising stochastic differential equations to non-Wiener processes is generalised. Non-Gaussian noise generated from a subset of Lévy processes can be used simply and often with more physical justification, for both additive and multiplicative noise. An example of this is provided that gives superior physical results compared to using geometric Brownian motion. Finally the results of the additive noise are shown to be equivalent to a derived master equation via the Kramers-Moyal expansion.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes the Euler-Maruyama discretization method to non-Wiener (Lévy) processes for simulating stochastic systems, showing that non-Gaussian noise from Lévy processes can provide more physically justified results than traditional Wiener-based approaches, with equivalence to a master equation via Kramers-Moyal expansion.
AI.motivation: Complex physical/biological systems often involve non-Gaussian fluctuations from non-Wiener processes, but these remain less explored due to lack of suitable simulation methods.
AI.method: Generalizes the Euler-Maruyama discretization method to non-Wiener processes (specifically a subset of Lévy processes), applicable to both additive and multiplicative noise.
AI.result: Non-Gaussian Lévy noise yields superior physical results compared to geometric Brownian motion in the provided example; additive noise results are equivalent to a master equation derived via the Kramers-Moyal expansion.
AI.conclusion: Lévy processes offer a simple, physically justified alternative to Wiener processes for simulating stochastic contributions in complex systems.

title: Enhanced Ionic Conductivity of confined Ionic-Liquid in Angstrom-scale 2D channels
summary: Understanding ion-transport under molecular confinement is essential for developing next-generation energy technologies, where ionic motion often occurs within nanoscale or angstrom-scale channels. In this study, we use the model system of 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide ([EMIM]+[TFSI]-) confined within angstrom-scale slit-shaped 2D channels fabricated via van der Waals assembly to exemplify a broader class of confined ionic liquids.This system provides a well-defined platform to unravel generic features of ion transport under extreme confinement. By systematically varying the channel height h, we demonstrate a non-monotonic conductivity dependence on confinement, with a maximum 26.7 S/m at confining height, 1.02 nm, over 30 times of the bulk value for these ionic liquids. The variation of conductivity with confinement arises from structural rearrangements of ionic layers in the slit channel. Enhanced values of conductivity occur under confinements that promote the breakup of ion pairs and larger clusters, thereby increasing the number of free ions. Stronger confinement (h, 0.68 nm) also leads to steric hindrance, lowering conductivity below bulk values. Furthermore, introducing co-solvents with a higher dielectric constant and lower viscosity, such as acetonitrile (ACN), amplifies conductivity to ~145 S/m. Comparative studies using ACN, dimethyl carbonate and diethyl carbonate highlight that both large dielectric constant and low viscosity critically govern ion transport under confinement, as also supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Overall, this work establishes confined [EMIM]+[TFSI]- as a representative system for probing mechanisms of nano- and angstrom-scale ion transport, demonstrating how nanoconfinement and the solvent environment can be systematically tuned to manipulate ionic conductivity at the molecular level.

AI.tldr: This study investigates ion transport in the ionic liquid [EMIM]+[TFSI]- confined within angstrom-scale 2D slit channels. Conductivity shows a non-monotonic dependence on confinement, peaking at 26.7 S/m (30× bulk) at 1.02 nm channel height, attributed to ion pair breakup. Stronger confinement (0.68 nm) reduces conductivity due to steric hindrance. Adding high-dielectric, low-viscosity co-solvents like acetonitrile boosts conductivity to ~145 S/m.
AI.motivation: Understanding ion transport under molecular confinement is essential for developing next-generation energy technologies, where ionic motion occurs within nanoscale or angstrom-scale channels.
AI.method: The study uses van der Waals assembly to fabricate angstrom-scale slit-shaped 2D channels, systematically varying channel height h to confine [EMIM]+[TFSI]- ionic liquid. Conductivity measurements are combined with comparative studies of co-solvents (ACN, DMC, DEC) and supported by molecular dynamics simulations.
AI.result: Non-monotonic conductivity dependence on confinement with a peak of 26.7 S/m at 1.02 nm (30× bulk value). Stronger confinement (0.68 nm) yields conductivity below bulk. Acetonitrile addition amplifies conductivity to ~145 S/m. Both high dielectric constant and low viscosity critically govern confined ion transport.
AI.conclusion: Confined [EMIM]+[TFSI]- serves as a representative system for probing nano- and angstrom-scale ion transport. Nanoconfinement and solvent environment can be systematically tuned to manipulate ionic conductivity at the molecular level.

title: Geometry-Driven Nonlinear Orbital Magnetoelectric Effect
summary: We propose a nonlinear orbital magnetoelectric effect, which generates orbital magnetization quadratically in centrosymmetric materials where the linear orbital magnetoelectric effect is strictly forbidden. Using extended semiclassical formulation, we derive a gauge-invariant microscopic theory that separates intrinsic and extrinsic contributions and establishes their distinct dependence on the relaxation time, providing an experimental discriminator. In two-dimensional systems the nonlinear response is far less constrained by out-of-plane rotational symmetries than the linear orbital magnetoelectric effect, substantially enlarging the materials platform. Microscopically, the dominant contributions are governed by a Hermitian-connection structure. Finally, we estimate that the magnitude of the nonlinear orbital magnetoelectric effect lies within the sensitivity of state-of-the-art magneto-optical Kerr measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a nonlinear orbital magnetoelectric effect that generates orbital magnetization quadratically in centrosymmetric materials, develops a gauge-invariant semiclassical theory separating intrinsic/extrinsic contributions, and shows the effect is measurable via magneto-optical Kerr techniques.
AI.motivation: Linear orbital magnetoelectric effect is forbidden in centrosymmetric materials, limiting the study of orbital magnetism in such systems; this work aims to unlock a nonlinear counterpart to access orbital magnetoelectric responses in centrosymmetric systems.
AI.method: Extended semiclassical formulation to derive a gauge-invariant microscopic theory; separation of intrinsic and extrinsic contributions with distinct relaxation-time dependence; analysis of symmetry constraints in 2D systems.
AI.result: Nonlinear orbital magnetoelectric effect generates orbital magnetization quadratic in the applied field; intrinsic and extrinsic contributions exhibit distinct relaxation-time scaling; effect is less symmetry-constrained than its linear counterpart in 2D; magnitude within sensitivity of magneto-optical Kerr measurements.
AI.conclusion: The nonlinear orbital magnetoelectric effect provides a viable route to study orbital magnetoelectric responses in centrosymmetric materials, with a broadened materials platform and experimental detectability via existing Kerr techniques.

title: Competition and coexistence of superconducting symmetries in $p$-wave magnets
summary: We investigate the interplay between unconventional magnetism and superconductivity in a model of a $p$-wave magnet on a square lattice. Using a self-consistent Bogoliubov-de-Gennes approach, we analyze the pairing amplitudes, competition, and coexistence of spin-singlet $s$-wave and spin-triplet $p$-wave pairings in the presence of a magnetic texture with a helical structure along the $x$ direction that is repeated in the $y$ direction. We find that the magnetic helix selectively stabilizes different pairing symmetries depending on its orientation and strength. In particular, mixed-spin $p_x$-wave pairing is enhanced at intermediate magnetic couplings and equal-spin $p_y$-wave pairing is robust and insensitive to all coupling intensities. When the multiple order parameters are simultaneously considered, we find regimes of coexistence and competition. Increasing the magnetic coupling drives two quantum phase transitions. The first from dominant spin-singlet $s$-wave to mixed-spin triplet $p_x$-wave pairings in a regime of coexistence. The second from spin-singlet $s$-wave and mixed-spin triplet $p$-wave pairings with total spin projection $S_z=0$ to dominant equal-spin triplet $p_y$-wave pairings with $S_z=\pm1$ in a regime of mutually exclusive superconducting phases. Our results demonstrate that $p$-wave magnetic order does not merely diminish spin-singlet $s$-wave superconductivity but can actively promote and stabilize spin-triplet $p$-wave pairing, both intrinsically and in proximity to spin-singlet $s$-wave superconductors. These findings highlight unconventional magnets as promising materials for realizing robust triplet superconductivity.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how a p-wave magnet on a square lattice affects superconductivity, finding that helical magnetic order can selectively stabilize different pairing symmetries—enhancing mixed-spin p_x-wave and robust equal-spin p_y-wave pairings—and drives two quantum phase transitions between singlet s-wave and triplet p-wave dominated regimes.
AI.motivation: To understand how unconventional (p-wave) magnetism interacts with superconductivity, particularly whether it can actively promote spin-triplet p-wave pairing rather than merely suppress singlet s-wave superconductivity.
AI.method: Self-consistent Bogoliubov-de-Gennes (BdG) approach on a square lattice model with a helical magnetic texture (periodic along x, repeated along y), analyzing pairing amplitudes, competition, and coexistence of s-wave and p-wave channels.
AI.result: Mixed-spin p_x-wave pairing is enhanced at intermediate magnetic couplings; equal-spin p_y-wave pairing is robust and insensitive to coupling intensity; two quantum phase transitions occur: (1) from dominant s-wave to mixed-spin p_x-wave with coexistence, (2) from s-wave & mixed-spin triplet (S_z=0) to equal-spin p_y-wave (S_z=±1) with mutual exclusion.
AI.conclusion: p-wave magnetic order can actively stabilize triplet p-wave pairing, both intrinsically and in proximity to s-wave superconductors, positioning unconventional magnets as promising platforms for robust triplet superconductivity.

title: $5/9-$Magnetization Plateau and Spin Supersolidity in YCu$_3$(OD)$_{7-x}$Br$_{2+x}$ under Magnetic Fields up to 120~T
summary: We performed high-precision magnetization measurements up to 120~T on three compositions of the newly discovered kagome antiferromagnet YCu$_3$(OD)$_{7-x}$Br$_{2+x}$ (YCOB), revealing a previously unobserved 5/9 fractional magnetization plateau. All YCOB samples with different Br$^-$ concentrations exhibit nearly identical magnetization curves below 60~T, whereas the 5/9 plateau appears at markedly different fields in the ultrahigh-field regime. By modeling the experimental data using tensor-network calculations, we derive the effective spin Hamiltonians for the YCOB family with three spatially anisotropic Heisenberg couplings (the 3$J$-type model), which quantitatively reproduces the measured magnetization processes and captures the composition-dependent evolution of the 5/9 plateau. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis suggests the emergence of a spin supersolid phase in the field window between the 1/3 and 5/9 plateaus, which is sensitive to spin exchange parameters and accounts for the significant variation in the critical fields of the 5/9 plateau observed among different YCOB compositions.

AI.tldr: This paper reports the discovery of a 5/9 fractional magnetization plateau in the kagome antiferromagnet YCu₃(OD)₇₋ₓBr₂₊ₓ (YCOB) under ultrahigh magnetic fields up to 120 T. Using tensor-network calculations, the authors derive a 3J-type anisotropic Heisenberg model that quantitatively captures the magnetization behavior, including composition-dependent evolution of the 5/9 plateau. Theoretical analysis further suggests a spin supersolid phase emerges between the 1/3 and 5/9 plateaus, explaining the observed variations in critical fields across different Br⁻ concentrations.
AI.motivation: To investigate high-field magnetization behavior in the newly discovered kagome antiferromagnet YCOB and uncover exotic quantum magnetic phases such as fractional magnetization plateaus and spin supersolids that were previously unobserved.
AI.method: High-precision magnetization measurements up to 120 T on three YCOB compositions with varying Br⁻ concentrations, combined with tensor-network calculations to model the data using a 3J-type anisotropic Heisenberg model with three spatially anisotropic couplings.
AI.result: Discovery of a previously unobserved 5/9 fractional magnetization plateau in YCOB; nearly identical magnetization below 60 T across compositions but markedly different plateau onset fields in ultrahigh fields; the 3J model quantitatively reproduces the magnetization curves and captures the composition-dependent evolution of the 5/9 plateau.
AI.conclusion: The 5/9 plateau is a robust feature of the YCOB family, and the theoretical analysis suggests a spin supersolid phase exists between the 1/3 and 5/9 plateaus, with its sensitivity to spin exchange parameters explaining the observed variation in critical fields among different compositions.

title: Percolation transition of strongly connected clusters in finite dimensions and on complete graphs
summary: We study the percolation of strongly connected clusters (SCCs), in which sites are mutually reachable through directed paths, in systems with randomly oriented bonds by extensive simulations on hypercubic lattices from dimension $d=2$ to $7$ and complete graphs. Below the upper critical dimension $d_u=6$, the critical SCCs exhibit nontrivial fractal dimension $d_{\rm SCC}$, and the size distribution scales as $\sim s^{-τ_{\rm SCC}}$ with the hyperscaling relation $τ_{\rm SCC}=1+d/d_{\rm SCC}$. For $d \ge d_u$, mean-field behavior is recovered with $d_{\rm SCC}/d=1/3$, consistent with complete-graph results. However, in contrast to hypercubic lattices, complete graphs exhibit a double-scaling structure in the SCC size distribution: large SCCs are governed by mean-field value $τ_{\rm SCC}=4$, while small SCCs follow a distinct power law with exponent $τ'=1$. At criticality, the giant in- and out-clusters are also fractal, sharing the same dimension as standard percolation clusters. These results show that critical SCCs remain well-defined fractal objects across dimensions, while their approach to the mean-field limit involves nontrivial changes in cluster statistics.

AI.tldr: This paper studies percolation of strongly connected clusters (SCCs) in randomly oriented bonds on hypercubic lattices (d=2-7) and complete graphs. Below the upper critical dimension d_u=6, SCCs exhibit nontrivial fractal dimension; above d_u, mean-field behavior emerges with d_SCC/d=1/3. Complete graphs show a double-scaling structure in SCC size distribution, with large SCCs following mean-field exponent τ=4 and small SCCs following τ'=1. Giant in- and out-clusters share the same fractal dimension as standard percolation clusters.
AI.motivation: To understand the percolation behavior of strongly connected clusters (SCCs) in systems with randomly oriented bonds across varying dimensions, particularly to determine critical behavior below and above the upper critical dimension d_u=6, and to compare results on hypercubic lattices with mean-field behavior on complete graphs.
AI.method: Extensive simulations on hypercubic lattices from d=2 to 7 and on complete graphs, analyzing SCC fractal dimensions, size distribution scaling exponents, and hyperscaling relations.
AI.result: Below d_u=6, SCCs have nontrivial fractal dimension d_SCC satisfying hyperscaling τ_SCC=1+d/d_SCC. For d≥6, mean-field behavior with d_SCC/d=1/3 emerges. Complete graphs exhibit a double-scaling structure: large SCCs follow τ=4 (mean-field), small SCCs follow τ'=1. Giant in- and out-clusters share fractal dimension with standard percolation.
AI.conclusion: Critical SCCs remain well-defined fractal objects across dimensions, with a nontrivial transition to mean-field behavior at d_u=6. Complete graphs show richer cluster statistics than hypercubic lattices, with a double-scaling size distribution.

title: Lattice Relaxation in Moiré Heterobilayers
summary: We develop an analytical theory for lattice relaxation in twisted moiré heterobilayers, accounting for lattice mismatch, twist, external biaxial heterostrain, and different elastic constants. Starting from continuum elasticity, we derive the self-consistent equations for the in-plane displacement fields and obtain simple perturbative expressions for the layer-resolved in-plane displacement fields induced by lattice relaxation. We apply our theory to graphene on hBN and representative 2H transition metal dichalcogenide heterobilayers, including MoTe$_2$/WSe$_2$ and WSe$_2$/WS$_2$. Our analytical results agree very well with full numerical solutions over experimentally relevant parameters. We further show that heterobilayers can exhibit a buckling instability near alignment, driven by compressive in-plane strain due to moiré relaxation. Our results provide a simple theoretical framework for incorporating lattice relaxation in realistic moiré heterostructures.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an analytical theory for lattice relaxation in twisted moiré heterobilayers, deriving perturbative expressions for displacement fields that agree well with numerical solutions, and predicting a buckling instability near alignment due to compressive in-plane strain.
AI.motivation: To develop a simple analytical framework for lattice relaxation in moiré heterobilayers that accounts for lattice mismatch, twist, external heterostrain, and different elastic constants, without relying on full numerical simulations.
AI.method: Starting from continuum elasticity theory, the authors derive self-consistent equations for in-plane displacement fields and obtain perturbative expressions. The theory is applied to graphene/hBN, MoTe₂/WSe₂, and WSe₂/WS₂ heterobilayers.
AI.result: Analytical results agree very well with full numerical solutions over experimentally relevant parameters. The theory also predicts a buckling instability near alignment driven by compressive in-plane strain from moiré relaxation.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a simple theoretical framework for incorporating lattice relaxation in realistic moiré heterostructures, enabling easier modeling of these systems.

title: I-V characteristics of SNS junctions with a multivalley normal region
summary: In multivalley conductors the inter-valley relaxation time $τ_v$ and the inelastic relaxation time $τ_{in}$ may be significantly longer than the intra-valley momentum relaxation time $τ$. We show that this separation of time scales has dramatic effects on the I-V characteristics of SNS junctions with a multivalley normal region. We generalize the Larkin-Ovchinnikov equations describing superconducting kinetics to the case of multivalley superconductors. We use this generalization to obtain a kinetic description of multivalley SNS junctions. We find that at constant voltage bias $V$, the current $I(V)$ is nonmonotonic; it exhibits two peaks of similar magnitude $I_\text{max,1} \sim I_\text{max,2}$ at $V_1 \sim \hbar(eτ_{in})^{-1}$ and $V_2\sim \hbar(eτ_v)^{-1}$, which may greatly exceed the critical current $I_c(T)$. At constant current bias $I$ we find that in a wide interval, $I_c(T) < I \lesssim I_{\text{jump}}$, the nonlinear resistance of the junction is controlled by the long relaxation times and may be several orders of magnitude smaller than the normal state resistance.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that multivalley SNS junctions exhibit nonmonotonic I-V characteristics with two current peaks at voltages set by inelastic and inter-valley relaxation times, and that under current bias the nonlinear resistance can be orders of magnitude smaller than normal state resistance due to long relaxation times.
AI.motivation: To understand how the separation of time scales (inter-valley relaxation time τ_v and inelastic relaxation time τ_{in} being much longer than intra-valley momentum relaxation time τ) affects the I-V characteristics of SNS junctions with a multivalley normal region.
AI.method: Generalization of the Larkin-Ovchinnikov equations describing superconducting kinetics to multivalley superconductors, followed by a kinetic description of multivalley SNS junctions.
AI.result: (1) At constant voltage bias V, the current I(V) is nonmonotonic with two peaks at V₁ ~ ℏ/(eτ_{in}) and V₂ ~ ℏ/(eτ_v), both comparable in magnitude and potentially much larger than the critical current I_c(T). (2) At constant current bias, for I_c(T) < I ≲ I_{jump}, the nonlinear resistance is controlled by long relaxation times and can be orders of magnitude below normal state resistance.
AI.conclusion: Long inter-valley and inelastic relaxation times in multivalley conductors produce striking effects on SNS junction transport, including nonmonotonic I-V curves and strongly suppressed nonlinear resistance.

title: Optical, vibrational, and electronic properties of semiconducting YbN
summary: We investigate the vibrational, optical, and electronic properties of insulating YbN thin films using Raman spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, and electrical transport measurements, supported by density functional theory. Raman spectra reveal the LO($Γ$) phonon and a cation-vacancy mode, while the optical conductivity identifies the TO phonon and an absorption edge corresponding to a 1.7 eV N 2p{$\rightarrow$}Yb 5d transition. The films exhibit thermally activated resistivity consistent with an insulating ground state. An additional defect induced absorption tail below the intrinsic band gap is observed, which in combination with the electrical measurements indicates the Fermi energy resides in a disordered conduction band minimum.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates YbN thin films, revealing insulating behavior with a 1.7 eV band gap, phonon modes, and defect-induced absorption tail indicating Fermi energy in a disordered conduction band minimum.
AI.motivation: To understand the vibrational, optical, and electronic properties of insulating YbN thin films, which are not well characterized.
AI.method: Raman spectroscopy, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, electrical transport measurements, and density functional theory calculations.
AI.result: Raman spectra show LO(Γ) phonon and cation-vacancy mode; optical conductivity reveals TO phonon and a 1.7 eV absorption edge (N 2p→Yb 5d). Films exhibit thermally activated resistivity. Defect-induced absorption tail below the band gap is observed.
AI.conclusion: YbN is an insulator with a 1.7 eV band gap, and the Fermi energy lies in a disordered conduction band minimum due to defects.

title: Exact Organization of Density Matrices and Entanglement Structure in the Kitaev Spin Liquid
summary: We give an exact form of the density matrix of the spin-1/2 Kitaev spin liquid represented in terms of spin operators and study the entanglement structures of the Kitaev honeycomb model within the spin framework. We show that the density matrix is naturally organized by equivalence classes of string operators associated with the underlying gauge structure of the model. With the explicit form of the density matrix, plus the exact Gauss law of the emergent gauge theory and the exact 1-form Wilson symmetry in the Kitaev model, we demonstrate the existence of the underlying symmetry-resolved block-diagonal structure of the reduced density matrix, which gives rise to the extensive degeneracy in the entanglement spectrum. The block-diagonal structure is then proven to be responsible for the separability of the entanglement entropy into the gauge and matter parts. Furthermore, we extend the formalism to subsystems with an odd number of lattice sites, revealing a relation between the entanglement spectrum and the fermion parity that is seldom mentioned in the literature.

AI.tldr: This paper derives an exact spin-operator form of the density matrix for the spin-1/2 Kitaev spin liquid, revealing symmetry-resolved block-diagonal structures in the reduced density matrix that lead to extensive degeneracy in the entanglement spectrum and a gauge-matter separable entanglement entropy, and extends the formalism to odd-sized subsystems to uncover a fermion parity relation.
AI.motivation: To provide an exact analytic description of the density matrix of the Kitaev spin liquid within the spin operator framework and to understand the entanglement structures arising from its underlying gauge symmetry, particularly the gauge-matter decomposition and entanglement spectrum degeneracy.
AI.method: The density matrix is expressed exactly using spin operators, organized by equivalence classes of string operators tied to the model's gauge structure. The analysis leverages the exact Gauss law of the emergent gauge theory and the exact 1-form Wilson symmetry to reveal a symmetry-resolved block-diagonal structure in the reduced density matrix, and extends to odd-site subsystems to examine fermion parity.
AI.result: The reduced density matrix exhibits a block-diagonal structure resolved by symmetry, causing extensive degeneracy in the entanglement spectrum. The entanglement entropy separates cleanly into gauge and matter contributions. For odd-sized subsystems, a relation between the entanglement spectrum and fermion parity is established.
AI.conclusion: The exact density matrix formalism, combined with the gauge symmetries of the Kitaev model, provides a complete understanding of its entanglement structure, including the origin of spectral degeneracy and entropy decomposition. The fermion parity relation for odd subsystems highlights a previously underexplored aspect of the entanglement spectrum.

title: Model of Simplicial Complexes with dimension-wise preferential attachment
summary: Network science is a powerful framework allowing to model complex systems, it is capable to describe and take into account the intricate web of connections existing among the constituting basic element of the system. Recently scholars have brought to the fore the relevance of higher-order networks, namely structures allowing to encode for many-body interaction, differently from the pairwise case handled by networks. This novel research field opens new avenues of research with applications ranging from neurosciences to social sciences; there is thus a need for generative models of higher-order network capable to reproduce features present in empirical data. In this work we present a model for growing simplicial complex rooted on a preferential attachment process acting dimension-wise, i.e., returning a power law distribution for the generalized degree of simplexes of different dimension.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a generative model for higher-order networks (simplicial complexes) based on a dimension-wise preferential attachment process that produces power law distributions for the generalized degree of simplexes, addressing the need for realistic generative models in fields like neuroscience and social sciences.
AI.motivation: Higher-order networks (simplicial complexes) are increasingly recognized as important for modeling many-body interactions in complex systems (e.g., neuroscience, social sciences), but there is a lack of generative models that can reproduce empirical features of such structures.
AI.method: A growing simplicial complex model based on a preferential attachment process acting dimension-wise, where attachment probability depends on the generalized degree of simplexes across different dimensions.
AI.result: The model returns a power law distribution for the generalized degree of simplexes across different dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed generative model successfully reproduces power law degree distributions observed in empirical higher-order networks, offering a useful tool for studying complex systems with many-body interactions.

title: Multiple Superconducting Phases in Rhombohedral Heptalayer Graphene
comment: To appear in Chin. Phys. Lett
summary: Crystalline rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG) has emerged as an ideal platform for studying unconventional superconductivity. Here, we report the observation of superconductivity in moiréless rhombohedral heptalayer graphene (RHG) at zero magnetic field. The superconducting phases emerge at low displacement electric fields (|D| < 0.2 V/nm) and are symmetrically distributed about D = 0, with one robust state exhibiting zero resistance and two weaker superconducting features. Comparisons with rhombohedral pentalayer graphene (RPG) reveal distinct perpendicular magnetic-field responses, and quantum oscillation measurements indicate that superconductivity in RHG arises from a half-metallic normal state. These results highlight the strong dependence of superconductivity on layer number and electronic structure in RMG systems and provide new insights into its microscopic origin.

AI.tldr: Superconductivity is observed in moiréless rhombohedral heptalayer graphene at zero magnetic field, emerging from a half-metallic normal state, with distinct layer-number-dependent behavior compared to pentalayer graphene.
AI.motivation: To investigate superconductivity in multilayer rhombohedral graphene without moiré patterns, and understand how layer number and electronic structure influence the superconducting state.
AI.method: Transport measurements of rhombohedral heptalayer graphene (RHG) at zero magnetic field, including quantum oscillations and comparison with rhombohedral pentalayer graphene (RPG) under perpendicular magnetic fields.
AI.result: Superconducting phases appear at low displacement fields (|D| < 0.2 V/nm), symmetric about D=0, with one robust zero-resistance state and two weaker features. RHG superconductivity arises from a half-metallic normal state, with distinct magnetic-field responses compared to RPG.
AI.conclusion: Superconductivity in RMG systems strongly depends on layer number and electronic structure; these findings offer new insights into the microscopic origin of superconductivity in rhombohedral multilayer graphene.

title: Hydrostatic Pressure-Induced Evolution of the Superconducting Transition Temperature of Bi-2212: Insights from First-Principles Calculations
summary: High-pressure experiments on Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_{8+x}$ (Bi-2212) have reported apparently conflicting evolutions of the superconducting transition temperature $T_c$, ranging from weak enhancement to strong suppression and even a proposed second superconducting dome. To clarify the origin of these discrepancies, we combine first-principles density functional theory calculations with a pressure-dependent low-energy bilayer model solved by the slave-boson mean-field method together with a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless estimate of phase coherence. Our results show that hydrostatic pressure induces a pronounced self-doping effect in Bi-2212: holes are transferred from the Bi-O charge-reservoir layers to the CuO$_2$ superconducting planes, leading to a systematic increase in the effective CuO$_2$-plane hole concentration $δ_x$. At the same time, pressure enhances the pairing scale through the renormalization of the hopping and superexchange parameters. As a consequence, the pressure evolution of $T_c$ is governed by the competition between pressure-enhanced pairing and pressure-driven motion along the common $T_c$-$δ_x$ dome, making $T_c(P)$ highly sensitive to the initial doping state. Even samples with very similar ambient-pressure $T_c$ but slightly different initial doping can therefore display qualitatively different pressure responses. This provides a unified interpretation of a large part of the disparate high-pressure behavior reported for Bi-2212 and suggests that slightly underdoped samples are more favorable than ambient-pressure optimal samples for achieving improved superconducting performance under pressure.
