AI.tldr: First-principles and slave-boson modeling reveal that hydrostatic pressure in Bi-2212 induces self-doping (hole transfer from Bi-O to CuO₂ layers) and enhanced pairing, causing Tc evolution to be highly sensitive to initial doping—explaining disparate experimental reports and suggesting underdoped samples are more favorable for pressure-enhanced superconductivity.
AI.motivation: To resolve conflicting experimental reports on how hydrostatic pressure affects Tc in Bi-2212 (ranging from weak enhancement to strong suppression to a proposed second superconducting dome).
AI.method: Combined first-principles DFT calculations with a pressure-dependent low-energy bilayer model solved via slave-boson mean-field theory and Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless phase coherence estimation.
AI.result: Pressure induces self-doping (hole transfer from Bi-O charge-reservoir layers to CuO₂ planes, increasing δx) and enhances pairing via renormalized hopping/superexchange; Tc(P) is governed by competition between enhanced pairing and motion along the Tc-δx dome, making it highly sensitive to initial doping.
AI.conclusion: Slightly underdoped samples are more favorable than ambient-pressure optimal samples for achieving improved superconducting performance under pressure, and the model unifies the disparate high-pressure behavior reported for Bi-2212.

title: Taming the 3D Wilson-Fisher Fixed Point via Nonlocal Effective Action
summary: We present a novel Renormalization Group (RG) framework based on a nonlocal effective action ansatz to tame the strong coupling dynamics of the three-dimensional relativistic $φ^{4}$ theory. By implementing a Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, we decouple the quartic interaction into a system of the primary field $φ$ and an auxiliary field $\varphi \sim φ^2$. Rather than freezing the intermediate scaling dimensions, the nonlocality of our effective action allows both exponents $Δ_φ$ and $Δ_{\varphi}$ to act as fully independent, unconstrained dynamical variables.This nonlocal propagator framework plays a critical role in the RG flow: evaluating self-energies and vertex fluctuations up to the three-loop order, the nonlocality drives precise structural cross-cancellations among multi-loop fluctuations near the Gaussian limit. Solving the resulting closed two-variable master equations isolates a robust, non-trivial physical fixed point at $Δ_φ^{*} \approx 0.981$ and $Δ_{\varphi}^{*} \approx 0.415$. These dynamic exponents yield a kinematic anomalous dimension $η_φ \approx 0.038$, an energy operator dimension $Δ_{φ^2} \approx 1.417$, and-via mass deformation-a thermal correlation length exponent $ν\approx 0.6317$, demonstrating exceptional quantitative agreement with high-precision Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) and conformal bootstrap benchmarks. Our results rigorously confirm that unfreezing the nonlocal degrees of freedom successfully eliminates the systematic truncation errors inherent to conventional local ansatz treatments, simultaneously resolving both the static scaling and thermodynamic flows of the Wilson-Fisher universality class.

AI.tldr: A novel nonlocal Renormalization Group framework for 3D φ⁴ theory, using a Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation to decouple the interaction, treats scaling dimensions as fully independent dynamical variables. Three-loop analysis yields fixed-point exponents Δ_φ*≈0.981, Δ_φ*≈0.415, giving η_φ≈0.038, Δ_{φ²}≈1.417, ν≈0.6317—matching high-precision QMC and conformal bootstrap results.
AI.motivation: Conventional local RG ansatz treatments suffer from systematic truncation errors when analyzing strongly coupled 3D φ⁴ theory; a framework that unfreezes nonlocal degrees of freedom is needed to eliminate these errors.
AI.method: Nonlocal effective action ansatz with Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation decoupling φ⁴ into φ and auxiliary field φ∼φ²; both scaling dimensions Δ_φ and Δ_φ treated as independent dynamical variables; self-energy and vertex evaluation up to three-loop order with structural cross-cancellations.
AI.result: Robust fixed point at Δ_φ*≈0.981, Δ_φ*≈0.415; η_φ≈0.038, Δ_{φ²}≈1.417, ν≈0.6317; exceptional agreement with QMC and conformal bootstrap benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Unfreezing nonlocal degrees of freedom eliminates systematic truncation errors of local treatments, simultaneously resolving static scaling and thermodynamic flows of the Wilson-Fisher universality class.

title: Path-Extrema Upper Bounds on Mean Entropy Production
summary: Fluctuation relations imply the second-law inequality $\langleΣ_T\rangle\ge0$, but path extrema can also constrain how large the mean entropy production can be. For steady-state processes with entropy-production martingale $M_t=e^{-Σ_t}$, we show that knowing only the positive running maximum of $Σ_t$ gives no improvement over the trivial endpoint bound: rare negative entropy-production excursions can still carry the exponential weight required by the fluctuation relation. Using the running extrema $L_T=\inf M_t$ and $H_T=\sup M_t$, we derive a path-extrema upper envelope $\mathcal{U}_{\rm ext}$. The relaxed envelope problem ranks realized intervals by the entropy gain per martingale cost, $\ln(H_T/L_T)/(H_T-L_T)$, giving a continuous knapsack problem. The actual mean satisfies the exact identity $\langleΣ_T\rangle=\mathcal{U}_{\rm ext}-\mathcal{A}-\mathcal{C}$, where $\mathcal{A}$ is an allocation gap across realized envelopes and $\mathcal{C}$ is a curvature gap within each envelope. Thus path extrema set the upper envelope, while the two gaps quantify how actual dynamics allocate terminal outcomes across envelope classes and place terminal values within each realized envelope. This turns path-extrema information into a quantitative upper-bound theory for entropy production, complementary to the usual lower-bound role of fluctuation relations.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that knowing only the positive running maximum of entropy production Σ_t does not improve over the trivial endpoint bound for mean entropy production. Using running extrema L_T and H_T of the martingale M_t=e^{-Σ_t}, the authors derive a path-extrema upper envelope and an exact identity ⟨Σ_T⟩ = U_ext - A - C, where A and C are allocation and curvature gaps, providing an upper-bound theory for entropy production complementary to fluctuation relations' lower-bound role.
AI.motivation: Fluctuation relations provide lower bounds on mean entropy production via the second-law inequality ⟨Σ_T⟩ ≥ 0, but upper bounds on how large mean entropy production can be are largely unexplored. The authors aim to develop a quantitative upper-bound theory for entropy production using path-extrema information.
AI.method: The authors analyze steady-state processes with the entropy-production martingale M_t=e^{-Σ_t}. They consider running extrema L_T=inf M_t and H_T=sup M_t, derive a path-extrema upper envelope U_ext, and formulate the relaxed envelope problem as a continuous knapsack problem ranking realized intervals by entropy gain per martingale cost ln(H_T/L_T)/(H_T-L_T). They derive an exact identity decomposing mean entropy production into the envelope minus allocation and curvature gaps.
AI.result: Knowing only the positive running maximum of Σ_t gives no improvement over the trivial endpoint bound due to rare negative entropy-production excursions. The mean entropy production satisfies ⟨Σ_T⟩ = U_ext - A - C, where A is an allocation gap across realized envelopes and C is a curvature gap within each envelope.
AI.conclusion: Path extrema set the upper envelope for mean entropy production, while allocation and curvature gaps quantify how actual dynamics allocate outcomes across envelope classes and place terminal values within each realized envelope. This provides a quantitative upper-bound theory for entropy production, complementary to the usual lower-bound role of fluctuation relations.

title: Causal Anomaly Detection for Lithium-Ion Battery Degradation
summary: Reliable early detection of lithium-ion battery degradation requires health indicators that are physically interpretable and computable from routine cycler telemetry without access to the degradation region. We introduce \textsc{CausalHealth}, a framework that applies causal graph discovery and $k$-nearest-neighbour transfer entropy to per-cycle voltage, current, temperature, and resistance time series, and organises twelve resulting anomaly scores into three signal-class bundles (Magnitude-shift, Predictive-residual, Complexity-entropy) -- with Isolation Forest reported separately as it falls below the bundle reliability threshold -- to characterise detection sensitivity across ten commissioning fractions (5--30\,\%). The Magnitude-shift class achieves 100\,\% detection across all seven tested cells spanning LFP (MIT--Stanford MATR) and LCO (NASA PCoE, CALCE CS2) chemistries, with a lead time of up to 402 cycles before conventional capacity-threshold failure on gradual-fade cells. A Reliability-Weighted Master Health Index (RWMHI) -- a cross-bundle fusion of five high-reliability detectors weighted by inverse coefficient of variation -- improves lead time by 15--52 cycles over the class median on long-lived cells while maintaining 100\,\% detection. Validation against electrochemical impedance spectroscopy on an NMC prismatic cell provides independent physical grounding: transfer entropy $\mathrm{TE}(R \!\to\! V)$ correlates with charge-transfer resistance $R_{\mathrm{ct}}$ (pooled $r = +0.990$; temperature-controlled partial $r = +0.898$), and an Arrhenius analysis of both quantities yields an activation energy consistent with published NMC charge-transfer kinetics. These results are evaluated on seven cells across three benchmark datasets.

AI.tldr: CausalHealth is a framework that uses causal graph discovery and transfer entropy on battery cycler data to generate three bundles of anomaly scores for early Li-ion battery degradation detection, achieving 100% detection across LFP and LCO chemistries with up to 402 cycles lead time, validated via EIS on NMC cells.
AI.motivation: Reliable early detection of lithium-ion battery degradation requires physically interpretable health indicators computable from routine cycler telemetry without needing access to the degradation region.
AI.method: Applies causal graph discovery and k-nearest-neighbour transfer entropy to per-cycle voltage, current, temperature, and resistance time series; organizes twelve anomaly scores into three signal-class bundles (Magnitude-shift, Predictive-residual, Complexity-entropy); fuses five high-reliability detectors via Reliability-Weighted Master Health Index (RWMHI) using inverse coefficient of variation weighting.
AI.result: Magnitude-shift class achieves 100% detection across LFP (MIT-Stanford MATR) and LCO (NASA PCoE, CALCE CS2) cells with up to 402 cycles lead time; RWMHI improves lead time by 15-52 cycles over class median on long-lived cells; transfer entropy TE(R→V) correlates with charge-transfer resistance (pooled r=+0.990, partial r=+0.898); Arrhenius analysis yields activation energy consistent with NMC charge-transfer kinetics.
AI.conclusion: CausalHealth provides physically grounded, high-reliability early detection of battery degradation across multiple chemistries, with validation against electrochemical impedance spectroscopy confirming the physical interpretability of the transfer entropy-based indicators.

title: Geometric symmetry and size-dependent skyrmion phase transitions in magnetic nanostructures
summary: We investigate the interplay of geometric symmetry, size, and external magnetic fields in regulating individual skyrmion states within magnetic nanostructures. By analyzing nanodisks, nanosquares, and nanorectangles, we demonstrate that rotational symmetry in nanodisks enables rich topological phase transitions, from ferromagnetic states to skyrmions, skyrmioniums, and multi-states, as their diameter increases. In contrast, square and rectangular structures exhibit suppressed topological complexity due to corner-induced demagnetization effects and reduced symmetries. Under perpendicular magnetic fields, nanodisks show field-driven transitions between skyrmionium and skyrmion states. By leveraging asymmetry, square and rectangular nanostructures stabilize skyrmions over a broader parameter range than nanodisks. These findings highlight geometric symmetry as a critical design parameter for tailoring skyrmion stability and functionality in spintronic applications such as multi-state memory and reconfigurable logic devices.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how geometric symmetry, size, and external magnetic fields regulate skyrmion states in magnetic nanostructures, showing that nanodisks enable rich topological transitions while square/rectangular structures suppress complexity but stabilize skyrmions over a broader parameter range.
AI.motivation: To understand how geometric symmetry, size, and external magnetic fields interplay in regulating individual skyrmion states within magnetic nanostructures, aiming to establish symmetry as a design parameter for spintronic applications.
AI.method: Analyzed three nanostructure geometries (nanodisks, nanosquares, nanorectangles) by varying their size and applying perpendicular magnetic fields, comparing rotational symmetry (disks) versus reduced symmetry with corner-induced demagnetization (squares/rectangles).
AI.result: Nanodisks exhibit rich topological phase transitions (ferromagnetic → skyrmions → skyrmioniums → multi-states) with increasing diameter; square/rectangular structures show suppressed topological complexity due to corner demagnetization and reduced symmetries; asymmetric structures stabilize skyrmions over a broader parameter range under perpendicular fields.
AI.conclusion: Geometric symmetry is a critical design parameter for tailoring skyrmion stability and functionality, with potential applications in multi-state memory and reconfigurable logic devices.

title: Observation of universal thermopolarization effect in insulators
summary: Heat-to-charge conversion has traditionally been realized via the Seebeck effect in conductors and pyroelectricity in polar insulators. Here, we demonstrate that temperature gradients generate electrical polarization, namely thermopolarization, in a wide range of insulators through a thermomechanical pathway. We identify a mechanism where thermal expansion under a temperature gradient produces strain gradients that induce polarization via the flexoelectric effect. Using a device with an on-chip heater, we detect the heat-induced polarization in crystalline, polymeric, and amorphous systems, including MgO, Al$_2$O$_3$, MnO, mica, PET, PEN, polyimide, and soda-lime glass. The magnitude of the response exhibits a robust scaling with the coefficient of thermal expansion, which is reproduced by finite-element simulations. Furthermore, we identify two routes to enhance the response: reducing the sample thickness and exploiting structural instabilities such as glass and antiferromagnetic phase transitions, where more than an order-of-magnitude enhancement is observed. These results establish a symmetry-independent route for heat-to-charge conversion in insulators and provide a device-compatible platform for electrically probing lattice responses, with potential for enhancement in nanoscale systems such as two-dimensional materials.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that temperature gradients generate electrical polarization (thermopolarization) in a wide range of insulators via a thermomechanical pathway involving thermal expansion-induced strain gradients and the flexoelectric effect, establishing a symmetry-independent route for heat-to-charge conversion.
AI.motivation: Traditional heat-to-charge conversion relies on the Seebeck effect (conductors) or pyroelectricity (polar insulators). The authors aim to demonstrate a general, symmetry-independent pathway for generating electrical polarization from temperature gradients in all insulators.
AI.method: The authors identify a mechanism where thermal expansion under a temperature gradient produces strain gradients that induce polarization via the flexoelectric effect. They build a device with an on-chip heater to detect heat-induced polarization in crystalline (MgO, Al₂O₃, MnO, mica), polymeric (PET, PEN, polyimide), and amorphous (soda-lime glass) systems. Finite-element simulations are used to reproduce the scaling behavior.
AI.result: The response magnitude scales robustly with the coefficient of thermal expansion. Enhancement is achieved via two routes: reducing sample thickness and exploiting structural instabilities (glass and antiferromagnetic phase transitions), where over an order-of-magnitude enhancement is observed.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a symmetry-independent, universal route for heat-to-charge conversion in insulators, providing a device-compatible platform for electrically probing lattice responses with potential for enhancement in nanoscale systems such as 2D materials.

title: Pressure Effects on CeMnSi: Evolution of Ce 4f and Mn 3d Electronic States and Negative Thermal Expansion
summary: We investigated pressure effects on the nontrivial heavy-fermion antiferromagnet CeMnSi by means of electrical resistivity and powder X-ray diffraction. With increasing pressure, the antiferromagnetic order of Mn (T_N ~ 240 K at ambient pressure) is rapidly suppressed and disappears at P_c ~ 1.3 GPa. Instead, a pressure-induced anomaly appears at T_M ~ 97 K and shifts to higher temperatures with increasing pressure. The switching of the Mn magnetic state may reflect a modification of the magnetic symmetry of the system, which could influence the stability of the heavy-fermion state. In the low-pressure region, non-Fermi-liquid-like behavior characterized by nearly T-linear resistivity is observed around 0.7 GPa. In addition, the resistivity shows a marked reduction below T_M and a qualitative change toward more metallic behavior above the structural transition pressure P_s ~ 5.7 GPa. At ambient pressure, CeMnSi exhibits negative thermal expansion below ~40 K, which is absent in LaMnSi, supporting the formation of a heavy-fermion ground state.

AI.tldr: This study investigates pressure effects on the heavy-fermion antiferromagnet CeMnSi, finding that Mn antiferromagnetic order is suppressed at ~1.3 GPa, a new anomaly appears at ~97 K, non-Fermi-liquid behavior emerges around 0.7 GPa, and negative thermal expansion below ~40 K supports heavy-fermion ground state formation.
AI.motivation: To understand how hydrostatic pressure modifies the magnetic order, electronic transport, and structural properties of the heavy-fermion antiferromagnet CeMnSi, particularly the interplay between Mn magnetism and the heavy-fermion state.
AI.method: Electrical resistivity measurements and powder X-ray diffraction under varying hydrostatic pressure conditions.
AI.result: Mn antiferromagnetic order (T_N ~ 240 K) is suppressed above P_c ~ 1.3 GPa; a pressure-induced anomaly at T_M ~ 97 K appears and shifts upward with pressure; non-Fermi-liquid-like nearly T-linear resistivity observed around 0.7 GPa; resistivity reduces markedly below T_M; more metallic behavior above P_s ~ 5.7 GPa; negative thermal expansion below ~40 K unique to CeMnSi (absent in LaMnSi).
AI.conclusion: Pressure tunes CeMnSi from an antiferromagnetic heavy-fermion state to a more metallic regime with a modified magnetic symmetry, potentially influencing heavy-fermion stability; negative thermal expansion corroborates the heavy-fermion ground state.

title: Exact solution and pair correlation functions for a generalized three-chain Ising tube with multispin interactions
summary: We obtain an exact solution for a generalized three-chain Ising tube (TCGIT) of length $L$ with toroidal boundary conditions and the most general $C_3$-invariant Hamiltonian on an elementary prism, containing 20 independent coupling constants, including an external magnetic field. Using an $8\times 8$ transfer matrix, we derive the exact partition function of the finite system and obtain the free energy, internal energy, specific heat, magnetization, magnetic susceptibility, and entropy in the thermodynamic limit $L\to\infty$. In the general case, $λ_{\max}$ is determined by a quartic equation, whereas in the principal special case with even-spin interactions (PSC) the spectrum simplifies substantially: the characteristic polynomial factorizes, and $λ_{\max}$ is given by the root of a quadratic equation. For mirror-symmetric subfamilies, we derive explicit formulas for the pair correlation functions and express the magnetization in terms of the components of the eigenvector associated with $λ_{\max}$; in the even-spin case with $h=0$, the magnetization vanishes. Important special cases include the width-three planar model with nearest-neighbor, next-nearest-neighbor, and plaquette interactions, including the entropy limit $S(T\to0^+)=(\ln 2)/3$ for $k\ge 0$ and $S(T\to0^+)=0$ for $k<0$, as well as the width-three planar triangular model with distinct nearest-neighbor couplings, three-spin interactions involving neighboring triangles, and an external field.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an exact solution for a generalized three-chain Ising tube model with 20 coupling constants, deriving thermodynamic quantities and correlation functions using an 8×8 transfer matrix, with simplifications in special cases.
AI.motivation: To obtain an exact solution for a generalized three-chain Ising tube (TCGIT) with the most general C₃-invariant Hamiltonian on an elementary prism, containing 20 independent coupling constants including an external magnetic field.
AI.method: An 8×8 transfer matrix approach is used to derive the exact partition function for finite systems, with thermodynamic limit (L→∞) taken afterward. The eigenvalue problem reduces to a quartic equation in the general case, and factorizes to a quadratic equation in the principal special case with even-spin interactions.
AI.result: In the general case, λ_max is determined by a quartic equation; in the principal special case (even-spin interactions), the characteristic polynomial factorizes and λ_max solves a quadratic equation. For mirror-symmetric subfamilies, explicit pair correlation functions are derived, and magnetization is expressed via eigenvector components; magnetization vanishes in the even-spin case with h=0. The entropy limit S(T→0⁺) = (ln 2)/3 for k≥0 and S(T→0⁺)=0 for k<0 is found for the width-three planar model.
AI.conclusion: The three-chain Ising tube model is exactly solvable with rich thermodynamic behavior, including special cases such as the width-three planar model with various interactions and the planar triangular model with distinct nearest-neighbor couplings, three-spin interactions, and external fields.

title: Charge order on a triangular lattice with Mott physics and arbitrary charge density
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 80 references; RevTeX class, double-column formatting; includes also Supplemental Material (3 pages, 4 figures)
summary: Triangular-lattice systems attract a lot of attention due to various frustration-induced and strongly correlated effects. Here, we focus on the charge-ordering phenomenon by means of investigation of the extended Hubbard model with dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). By considering the intersite nearest-neighbor interaction we have found a very rich phase diagram that contains large number of features, phases, and phase transitions. Among them are pinball-liquid (PL) phases where we distinguish charge-transfer-driven and Mott-localization-driven PLs; phase transitions that change their order as model parameters evolve (from discontinuous to continuous); very strong particle-hole asymmetry. Various features of the phase diagram are found to be better understood by means of the simple mean-field approximation (MFA). Moreover, besides helping with interpretation of the phase diagram, the MFA results together with results for the atomic-limit model are found to be able to set rather good expectations on how the DMFT phase diagram should look like. Nevertheless, a few features were not expected and are found within the DMFT, such as a small-region intermediate metallic phase on an electron-doped side of the phase diagram.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates charge ordering in the extended Hubbard model on a triangular lattice using dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), revealing a rich phase diagram with pinball-liquid phases, variable-order phase transitions, strong particle-hole asymmetry, and an unexpected intermediate metallic phase on the electron-doped side.
AI.motivation: Triangular-lattice systems attract attention due to frustration-induced and strongly correlated effects, and the authors aim to understand charge-ordering phenomena in this context.
AI.method: The authors study the extended Hubbard model with intersite nearest-neighbor interaction using dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT), supplemented by simple mean-field approximation (MFA) and atomic-limit model analysis.
AI.result: A rich phase diagram is found, including pinball-liquid (PL) phases (charge-transfer-driven and Mott-localization-driven), phase transitions that change order (discontinuous to continuous), strong particle-hole asymmetry, and a small-region intermediate metallic phase on the electron-doped side not anticipated by MFA or atomic-limit models.
AI.conclusion: MFA and atomic-limit results provide good qualitative guidance for the DMFT phase diagram, but DMFT reveals unexpected features (e.g., the intermediate metallic phase) that cannot be captured by simpler approximations.

title: Multi-rotational switching in a noncollinear antiferromagnet by spin-orbit torque
summary: Spintronics has advanced through discoveries of various electrically-driven spin dynamics in nanomagnets. Here, we report a novel switching dynamics of spin systems driven by spin-orbit torque, using a noncollinear antiferromagnetic nanodot. With electric pulses spanning a wide range of durations and amplitudes, we find an unconventional insensitivity of a threshold current density to pulse duration in switch-back events. This observation is attributed to a previously unrecognized process, in which the noncollinear antiferromagnetic order undergoes multiple rotations before completing reversal, a phenomenon we term multi-rotational switching. Our theoretical analysis reveals that multi-rotational switching arises from the interplay of three key factors: current-driven coherent rotation of the noncollinear antiferromagnetic order, field-induced reorientation of the uncompensated net magnetization, and thermal fluctuations. These findings establish a microscopic mechanism governing current-induced switching in noncollinear antiferromagnets, a topic of growing interest for next-generation spintronics technologies, opening a new route to controlling antiferromagnetic order in nanodevices.

AI.tldr: This paper reports a novel multi-rotational switching dynamics in noncollinear antiferromagnetic nanodots driven by spin-orbit torque, where threshold current density is insensitive to pulse duration due to multiple rotations of antiferromagnetic order before reversal, arising from interplay of coherent rotation, field-induced reorientation, and thermal fluctuations.
AI.motivation: To discover and understand the switching dynamics of spin systems driven by spin-orbit torque in noncollinear antiferromagnetic nanodots, particularly the unconventional insensitivity of threshold current density to pulse duration, which is important for next-generation spintronics technologies.
AI.method: Experimental observation of switching dynamics in noncollinear antiferromagnetic nanodots using electric pulses with varying durations and amplitudes, combined with theoretical analysis to explain the underlying mechanism of multi-rotational switching.
AI.result: Discovery of multi-rotational switching where noncollinear antiferromagnetic order undergoes multiple rotations before completing reversal, leading to unconventional insensitivity of threshold current density to pulse duration in switch-back events.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a microscopic mechanism governing current-induced switching in noncollinear antiferromagnets, opening a new route to controlling antiferromagnetic order in nanodevices for next-generation spintronics.

title: Direction-selective triplet pairing and spin-edge locking in altermagnetic metals
summary: We investigate self-consistent unconventional superconductivity in a two-dimensional $d$-wave altermagnetic metal. We find that momentum-dependent altermagnetic spin splitting suppresses opposite-spin singlet pairing and stabilizes highly anisotropic equal-spin triplet order. In the spin-conserving limit, this directional triplet pairing gives rise to nearly dispersionless Majorana boundary states associated with effective one-dimensional topological channels. Rashba spin-orbit coupling mixes spin sectors, activates additional pairing components, and drives the system into a mixed-parity superconducting state with dispersive Majorana boundary states. The spin-resolved boundary spectra further reveal a characteristic locking between boundary orientation and spin polarization, reflecting the underlying altermagnetic symmetry. These results identify altermagnetic spin splitting as an intrinsic mechanism for selecting unconventional pairing and generating spin-resolved Majorana boundary states without external magnetic fields.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that altermagnetic spin splitting in d-wave altermagnetic metals can stabilize equal-spin triplet superconductivity and generate spin-resolved Majorana boundary states without external magnetic fields.
AI.motivation: To understand how the unique momentum-dependent spin splitting in altermagnets influences unconventional superconductivity, particularly the selection of pairing symmetry and the emergence of topological boundary states without external magnetic fields.
AI.method: The authors theoretically investigate self-consistent unconventional superconductivity in a two-dimensional d-wave altermagnetic metal, analyzing the effects of altermagnetic spin splitting on pairing channels, and examining the interplay with Rashba spin-orbit coupling to determine the resulting superconducting order parameters and boundary state spectra.
AI.result: Altermagnetic spin splitting suppresses opposite-spin singlet pairing and stabilizes highly anisotropic equal-spin triplet order. In the spin-conserving limit, nearly dispersionless Majorana boundary states emerge from effective 1D topological channels. Rashba spin-orbit coupling mixes spin sectors, activates additional pairing components, and produces dispersive Majorana boundary states with a characteristic locking between boundary orientation and spin polarization.
AI.conclusion: Altermagnetic spin splitting serves as an intrinsic mechanism for selecting unconventional (triplet) pairing and generating spin-resolved Majorana boundary states without needing external magnetic fields.

title: On-chip detection of anisotropic thermopolarization in quartz
summary: Temperature gradients are widely used to drive and probe transport phenomena in solids, forming the basis of heat-to-charge conversion processes. In typical experiments, local heating is introduced to generate a temperature gradient, and the resulting electrical response is detected by separate electrodes. Such measurements usually regard heating purely as a source of thermal excitation. Here, we show that heating inherently generates mechanical stress through thermal expansion, which in turn produces measurable electrical signals via electromechanical coupling. Using quartz as a model piezoelectric system, we demonstrate that heat can be converted to electrical currents via thermally generated stress. The on-chip device used in our experiment enables us to probe the anisotropy of the piezoelectric tensor through the thermally generated current, exhibiting twofold and threefold responses for X-cut and Z-cut crystals, respectively. We further show that the response can be detected in both current and voltage modes. These results reveal a thermomechanical pathway for heat-to-charge conversion and establish a general platform for electrically probing thermomechanical responses in insulating materials.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that heating generates mechanical stress via thermal expansion, which produces electrical signals through electromechanical coupling in piezoelectric materials, revealing a thermomechanical pathway for heat-to-charge conversion using quartz as a model system.
AI.motivation: To show that heating inherently generates mechanical stress through thermal expansion, which can produce measurable electrical signals via electromechanical coupling—challenging the conventional view that heating purely serves as a source of thermal excitation in heat-to-charge conversion experiments.
AI.method: Using quartz as a model piezoelectric system, the authors employ an on-chip device to probe the anisotropy of the piezoelectric tensor through thermally generated current, measuring both twofold (X-cut) and threefold (Z-cut) crystal responses in current and voltage modes.
AI.result: Heat can be converted to electrical currents via thermally generated stress; the on-chip device probes piezoelectric tensor anisotropy with twofold and threefold responses for X-cut and Z-cut quartz crystals, detectable in both current and voltage modes.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a thermomechanical pathway for heat-to-charge conversion and establish a general platform for electrically probing thermomechanical responses in insulating materials.

title: Variational Boundary Fluctuations as a First-Principles Origin of Langevin Noise
summary: Stochastic forces are usually postulated or obtained by eliminating environmental degrees of freedom. Here we identify a variational origin: fluctuating endpoint data in Hamilton's principle induce fluctuations of the on-shell action. Hamilton--Jacobi propagation transports this boundary imprint, whose gradient generates an effective Langevin force inherited from boundary-action fluctuations. The resulting force is not freely specifiable: its amplitude is filtered by the Hessian of Hamilton's principal function, yielding multiplicative and state-dependent noise. Homogeneous additive Langevin forcing is recovered only as a Markovian coarse-grained limit.

AI.tldr: This paper identifies a variational origin for stochastic forces: fluctuating endpoint data in Hamilton's principle lead to on-shell action fluctuations. These propagate via Hamilton-Jacobi theory, generating effective Langevin forces that are multiplicative, state-dependent, and filtered by the Hessian of Hamilton's principal function. Homogeneous additive noise only emerges as a Markovian coarse-grained limit.
AI.motivation: Typically, stochastic forces are introduced ad hoc or derived from eliminating environmental degrees of freedom. The authors seek a more fundamental variational origin rooted in Hamilton's principle itself.
AI.method: The authors analyze how fluctuating endpoint data in Hamilton's principle induce on-shell action fluctuations. They employ Hamilton-Jacobi theory to propagate these boundary imprints, showing that the gradient of the fluctuating action generates an effective Langevin force. The relationship between boundary fluctuations and resulting stochastic forces is derived via the Hessian of Hamilton's principal function.
AI.result: The resulting Langevin force is not freely specifiable; its amplitude is filtered by the Hessian of Hamilton's principal function, producing multiplicative and state-dependent noise. Pure additive homogeneous Langevin forcing is only recovered in a Markovian coarse-grained limit.
AI.conclusion: Stochastic forces can have a variational origin from fluctuating boundary data in Hamilton's principle, offering a principled alternative to ad hoc postulation or elimination methods. The noise structure is inherently constrained by the system's dynamics and is generally multiplicative rather than additive.

title: Strong nanomechanical Duffing nonlinearity and interactions induced through cavity optomechanics
summary: Nonlinearity is a key resource in both classical and quantum signal processing. Nonlinear nanomechanical elements have found applications ranging from sensing to computing, while networks of nonlinear resonators, as well as nonlinearly coupled networks of linear resonators, constitute promising platforms for simulating complex dynamics. Here, we experimentally demonstrate an approach to realizing strong mechanical nonlinearity in nanomechanical resonators, fully controlled through optical laser drives. The mechanism exploits the nonlinearity of the radiation-pressure interaction in a cavity optomechanical system, which gives rise to a nonlinear optical spring effect. The resulting Duffing nonlinearity is conveniently tunable in strength via pump laser power, while its sign is controlled by laser detuning. Moreover, we demonstrate that the nonlinear optical spring mediates effective interactions between mechanical modes coupled to a common cavity, inducing tunable nonlinear interactions between them that impact spectral response and dynamics. These results establish cavity optomechanics as a versatile and in-situ reconfigurable platform for engineering nonlinear dynamics in resonators and networks.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a cavity optomechanics approach to realize strong, tunable mechanical nonlinearity (Duffing-type) via radiation-pressure-induced nonlinear optical spring effect, with sign and strength controlled by laser detuning and power. It also shows this nonlinearity mediates tunable interactions between multiple mechanical modes coupled to a common optical cavity.
AI.motivation: Nonlinearity is a key resource for signal processing, sensing, computing, and simulating complex dynamics, but achieving strong, controllable mechanical nonlinearity in nanomechanical resonators remains challenging.
AI.method: The approach exploits the intrinsic nonlinearity of radiation-pressure interaction in cavity optomechanics to generate a nonlinear optical spring effect, producing a Duffing nonlinearity whose strength is tuned by pump laser power and sign by laser detuning.
AI.result: Demonstrated fully optically controlled, strong mechanical nonlinearity with tunable strength and sign, and showed that the nonlinear optical spring mediates effective tunable nonlinear interactions between multiple mechanical modes sharing a common cavity.
AI.conclusion: Cavity optomechanics provides a versatile, in-situ reconfigurable platform for engineering nonlinear dynamics in resonators and networks.

title: Phase dynamics and dissipation in tunnel ferromagnetic Josephson junctions
summary: We investigate tunnel ferromagnetic Josephson junctions based on Superconductor-Insulator-thin superconductor-Ferromagnet-Superconductor multilayers. A comparative study of their electrodynamic properties is performed for junctions with niobium and aluminum (Al) electrodes, featuring different ferromagnetic interlayer materials and lateral dimensions ranging from the micrometric to the submicrometric scale. The parameters extracted from the fitting of the current-voltage characteristics using the tunnel junction microscopic model are found to be consistent with those independently estimated from switching current distribution measurements. Submicrometric Al-based devices exhibit electrodynamic properties comparable to those implemented in state-of-the-art transmon qubits and display clear signatures of quantum phase diffusion. The strong agreement between transport modelling and escape dynamics establishes a robust framework for describing hybrid ferromagnetic Josephson junctions consistent with their energy scales and supports their potential integration into superconducting quantum and classical digital circuits.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates tunnel ferromagnetic Josephson junctions with Nb and Al electrodes, comparing their electrodynamic properties across different sizes and ferromagnetic interlayers. Parameters from current-voltage fitting align with switching current measurements. Submicrometric Al devices show quantum phase diffusion signatures comparable to transmon qubits, supporting integration into quantum and classical circuits.
AI.motivation: To understand and characterize the electrodynamic properties of ferromagnetic Josephson junctions for potential integration into superconducting quantum and classical digital circuits.
AI.method: Comparative study of Superconductor-Insulator-thin superconductor-Ferromagnet-Superconductor multilayers with Nb and Al electrodes, using tunnel junction microscopic model fitting of current-voltage characteristics and switching current distribution measurements across micrometric to submicrometric scales.
AI.result: Parameters from current-voltage fitting are consistent with switching current distribution measurements. Submicrometric Al-based devices exhibit electrodynamic properties comparable to state-of-the-art transmon qubits with clear quantum phase diffusion signatures.
AI.conclusion: The strong agreement between transport modelling and escape dynamics establishes a robust framework for describing hybrid ferromagnetic Josephson junctions, supporting their integration into superconducting quantum and classical digital circuits.

title: Frequency renormalization and its effects in nonlinear phononics with $Q_RQ_{IR}^{2}$-type coupling
summary: A two-phonon system with lowest-order coupling of form $Q_RQ_{IR}^2$ is studied by perturbation method, and analytic results for both phonon displacements and frequencies are obtained. The frequency renormalization of infrared (IR) active mode brings the rectification of Raman mode to saturate at high pump field. For degenerate IR mode with coupling of form $Q_R(Q_{IR,x}^2-Q_{IR,y}^2)$, the frequency of IR mode will split when resonantly pumped by elliptically or linearly polarized ultrashort mid-IR pulse, realizing Raman rectification and magnetization simultaneously. Our results reveal a dynamical effect of nonlinear phononics not captured by first-principles calculation, extend the dynamical multiferroicity to systems with coupling $Q_R(Q_{IR,x}^2-Q_{IR,y}^2)$, and the method can be readily applied to higher-order couplings. The amplitude saturation under strong pump field stimulates future researches to overcome this nonlinear effect.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a two-phonon system with nonlinear couplings using perturbation methods, revealing saturation of Raman rectification at high pump fields, frequency splitting of degenerate IR modes under elliptically/linearly polarized pulses, and extension of dynamical multiferroicity to new coupling forms.
AI.motivation: To understand nonlinear phononics beyond first-principles calculations, particularly the saturation behavior and frequency splitting effects in two-phonon systems with specific coupling forms.
AI.method: Perturbation method analyzing two-phonon systems with lowest-order coupling $Q_RQ_{IR}^2$ and degenerate IR coupling $Q_R(Q_{IR,x}^2-Q_{IR,y}^2)$ under strong mid-IR pump pulses.
AI.result: Frequency renormalization of IR mode leads to saturation of Raman rectification at high pump fields; degenerate IR modes exhibit frequency splitting under elliptically or linearly polarized pumping, simultaneously producing Raman rectification and magnetization.
AI.conclusion: Revealed a dynamical nonlinear phononics effect beyond DFT calculations, extended dynamical multiferroicity to $Q_R(Q_{IR,x}^2-Q_{IR,y}^2)$ coupling systems, and identified amplitude saturation as a challenge for future research.

title: Iterative maps emerging from cohomological structure of primes
summary: Prime numbers appeared in contexts spanning statistical mechanics, quantum mechanics and dynamical systems. However, the mechanisms governing the irregularities observed in their sequence and linking them to physical systems remained unclear. Here, it is shown that prime gaps at different separation distances follow a function depending on that distance and can be described by an iterative map which predicts the primary growth of successive primes. On the other hand, the analysis of remaining fluctuations reveals the existence of a well-defined cohomological structure, where the deterministic functional relation holds for primes up to small decaying fluctuations. In consequence, the long-range correlations as well as local jumps in primes encode the underlying cohomological structure where prime numbers are states of a given system that becomes deterministic asymptotically. Remarkably, the solution to this cohomological equation turns out to be the logarithmic integral function.

AI.tldr: Prime gaps follow a deterministic function described by an iterative map, with remaining fluctuations revealing a cohomological structure whose solution is the logarithmic integral function, making primes asymptotically deterministic states of a physical system.
AI.motivation: To uncover the mechanisms governing irregularities in prime number sequences and link them to physical systems across statistical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and dynamical systems.
AI.method: Analyzing prime gaps at different separation distances using an iterative map to describe primary growth, and applying cohomological analysis to remaining fluctuations.
AI.result: Prime gaps follow a distance-dependent function; fluctuations encode a cohomological structure where the deterministic functional relation holds up to small decaying fluctuations; the cohomological equation's solution is the logarithmic integral function.
AI.conclusion: Prime numbers behave like states of a physical system that becomes deterministic asymptotically, with long-range correlations and local jumps encoding an underlying cohomological structure.

title: Kapitza-like modulation of near-field radiative heat transfer
summary: We introduce a Kapitza-like mechanism for the near-field radiative heat transfer and show that fast modulation of any parameter controlling the flux, such as the vacuum gap or a material response, produces a quadratic, time-averaged correction in the slow thermal dynamics. This correction splits into a frequency-independent static term and a low-pass dynamical term, yielding sizable modulation-induced temperature shifts and modified effective thermal conductances that can stabilize or destabilize the steady state. Applying the theory to gap modulation between SiC slabs, we derive analytical scaling laws and predict temperature shifts that are fully measurable with existing experimental platforms, requiring only readily accessible low modulation frequencies of order $Ω\approx 10^4~\mathrm{rad/s}$. Our results establish a thermal analogue of the Kapitza mechanism and provide a general route for controlling radiative heat flow in micro- and nanoscale platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Kapitza-like mechanism for near-field radiative heat transfer, showing that fast modulation of parameters (e.g., gap, material response) creates a quadratic time-averaged correction to slow thermal dynamics, leading to measurable temperature shifts and modified thermal conductances, with application to SiC slabs demonstrating feasibility at low modulation frequencies (~10^4 rad/s).
AI.motivation: To establish a thermal analogue of the Kapitza mechanism (modulation-induced quadratic corrections) for near-field radiative heat transfer and provide a general route for controlling radiative heat flow at micro- and nanoscales.
AI.method: The authors derive a theory where fast modulation of any flux-controlling parameter (e.g., vacuum gap, material response) produces a quadratic time-averaged correction. The correction splits into a static (frequency-independent) term and a low-pass dynamical term. They apply the theory to gap modulation between SiC slabs and derive analytical scaling laws.
AI.result: Modulation yields sizable temperature shifts and modified effective thermal conductances that can stabilize or destabilize the steady state. For SiC slabs, predicted temperature shifts are fully measurable with existing experimental platforms at low modulation frequencies ~10^4 rad/s.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a thermal analogue of the Kapitza mechanism, providing a general approach for controlling radiative heat flow in micro- and nanoscale platforms via parameter modulation.

title: Interlayer electronic coherence links magnetism and superconductivity in Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates
summary: The extent to which electronic dimensionality influences magnetism and superconductivity in Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates remains unsettled. Here we report high-precision crystallographic-axis-resolved dc transport measurements on high-quality single crystals of bilayer and trilayer RP nickelates. Using a six-terminal geometry, we self-consistently determine the intrinsic in-plane ($ρ_\parallel$) and out-of-plane ($ρ_\bot$) resistivities on the same crystal, while minimizing uncertainties associated with current redistribution in highly anisotropic conductors. We uncover strong intrinsic electronic anisotropy in both bilayer and trilayer nickelates, in contrast to the weak anisotropy inferred from conventional four-probe measurements. Moreover, $ρ_\bot$ exhibits a nonmonotonic temperature dependence, revealing a universal coherent-to-incoherent crossover in interlayer transport. Across the RP nickelate series, the maximum superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$) observed under pressure is inversely correlated with the ambient-pressure resistivity anisotropy, suggesting that stronger interlayer electronic coherence is favorable for superconductivity. In addition, $ρ_\bot$ serves as an exceptionally sensitive and selective probe of magnetic and density-wave orders, exhibiting pronounced anomalies, whereas only weak signatures are observed in $ρ_\parallel$. Our results highlight interlayer coherence as a key organizing parameter that both tracks the relevant magnetic correlations and is closely tied to superconductivity, providing stringent constraints on microscopic theories of high-$T_c$ superconductivity in nickelates.

AI.tldr: This paper reports high-precision transport measurements on bilayer and trilayer Ruddlesden-Popper nickelate single crystals, revealing strong electronic anisotropy, a coherent-to-incoherent crossover in interlayer transport, and an inverse correlation between resistivity anisotropy and superconducting Tc under pressure, establishing interlayer coherence as a key parameter linking magnetism and superconductivity.
AI.motivation: To resolve the unsettled question of how electronic dimensionality affects magnetism and superconductivity in Ruddlesden-Popper nickelates, by directly measuring intrinsic in-plane and out-of-plane resistivities on the same high-quality single crystals with minimized measurement artifacts.
AI.method: High-precision crystallographic-axis-resolved DC transport using a six-terminal geometry on high-quality single crystals of bilayer and trilayer RP nickelates, enabling self-consistent determination of intrinsic ρ∥ and ρ⊥ while minimizing errors from current redistribution in anisotropic conductors.
AI.result: Strong intrinsic electronic anisotropy is found in both bilayer and trilayer nickelates, contrasting with weak anisotropy from conventional four-probe measurements. ρ⊥ shows a nonmonotonic temperature dependence indicating a universal coherent-to-incoherent crossover. Maximum superconducting Tc under pressure is inversely correlated with ambient-pressure resistivity anisotropy. ρ⊥ exhibits pronounced anomalies for magnetic/density-wave orders while ρ∥ shows only weak signatures.
AI.conclusion: Interlayer coherence is a key organizing parameter that tracks magnetic correlations and is closely tied to superconductivity, providing stringent constraints on microscopic theories of high-Tc superconductivity in nickelates.

title: Theory of melting lines with a variable enthalpy of fusion
summary: Conventional derivations of phase boundaries from the Clausius-Clapeyron (CC) relation often employ the constant latent heat approximation to maintain analytical functions of the sublimation and boiling curves. To address the complex thermodynamics of the solid-liquid transition, we develop a two-phase analytical model by modifying the CC equation to account for a variable enthalpy of fusion along the melting line (ML). Our methodology utilizes recent theoretical and experimental progress demonstrating that the isobaric heat capacity of crystalline solids near the melting point features a dominant anharmonic, volume-dependent component. Consequently, the latent heat is correlated to the specific volumes of the coexisting phases. Differentiation of this modified CC relation yields a second-order differential equation governing ML. By imposing appropriate e boundary conditions, physically acceptable approximate parabolic solutions are derived. The parameters of these analytic functions are defined exclusively by fundamental thermophysical properties, including the bulk moduli, thermal expansion coefficients, and specific volumes of the coexisting phases, as well as the isobaric heat capacity of the solid. Our derivation, rooted in solid-state anharmonicity, yields approximate parabolic scaling laws that corroborate with a recent universal model derived from the Phonon Theory of Liquids [K. Trachenko, Phys. Rev. E 109, 034122 (2024)], supporting the universal parabolic nature of melting curves from a completely distinct theoretical foundation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a two-phase analytical model for melting curves by modifying the Clausius-Clapeyron relation to account for variable latent heat, incorporating solid-state anharmonicity, and derives approximate parabolic scaling laws that align with a recent universal model from Phonon Theory of Liquids.
AI.motivation: Conventional Clausius-Clapeyron derivations assume constant latent heat for analytical tractability, which fails to capture the complex thermodynamics of solid-liquid transitions. A more accurate model accounting for variable enthalpy of fusion along the melting line is needed.
AI.method: The CC equation is modified to incorporate variable latent heat by correlating it to specific volumes of coexisting phases, based on the finding that the isobaric heat capacity of crystalline solids near melting has a dominant anharmonic, volume-dependent component. Differentiation yields a second-order ODE for the melting line, solved with appropriate boundary conditions to obtain approximate parabolic solutions.
AI.result: Analytic parabolic functions for melting curves are derived, with parameters defined solely by fundamental thermophysical properties (bulk moduli, thermal expansion coefficients, specific volumes of coexisting phases, and isobaric heat capacity of the solid).
AI.conclusion: The derivation from solid-state anharmonicity yields parabolic scaling laws that corroborate a recent universal model from Phonon Theory of Liquids, supporting the universal parabolic nature of melting curves from a distinct theoretical foundation.

title: Qumus: Realization of An Embodied AI Quantum Material Experimentalist
comment: 29 Pages in total. Supplementary Demo Videos are available at https://qumus.ai
summary: While modern Large Language Models (LLMs) and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) have demonstrated transformative capabilities in digital domains, the realization of embodied AI capable of real-world scientific discovery remains a difficult frontier. The advancements are hindered by the inherent complexity of integrating high-level reasoning, multimodal information processing and real-time physical execution. Here we introduce Qumus, the first AI quantum materials experimentalist. Physically embodied within a robotic mini-laboratory, Qumus is an intelligent, multimodal, and multi-agent system designed for the creation and nano-processing of atomically thin two-dimensional (2D) materials and stacked van der Waals (vdW) structures. Qumus autonomously navigates the full scientific cycle, from hypothesis generation and protocol planning to multi-step experimental execution, result analysis and reporting, acting as an experimentalist. Markedly, the system has achieved, for the first time, the AI-creation of graphene, as well as the first AI-fabrication of complex nanodevices including atomically thin field-effect transistors via vdW stacking. Qumus excels at these tasks by demonstrating autonomous error correction and closed-loop experimentation. Our results establish a generalizable framework for self-improving embodied AI systems that learn directly from the quantum world, opening a pathway toward accelerated discovery in quantum materials, electronics and beyond.

AI.tldr: Qumus is the first AI quantum materials experimentalist—an embodied, multimodal, multi-agent robotic system that autonomously performs the full scientific cycle (hypothesis generation, planning, execution, analysis, reporting) for creating 2D materials and van der Waals structures. It achieved the first AI-creation of graphene and AI-fabrication of atomically thin transistors, demonstrating autonomous error correction and closed-loop experimentation.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between LLM-driven AI capabilities in digital domains and the realization of embodied AI that can autonomously perform real-world scientific discovery in quantum materials, overcoming the challenges of integrating high-level reasoning, multimodal perception, and physical execution.
AI.method: Qumus is physically embodied as a robotic mini-laboratory, employing a multimodal, multi-agent system that integrates hypothesis generation, protocol planning, multi-step experimental execution, result analysis, and reporting. It uses closed-loop experimentation and autonomous error correction to navigate the full scientific cycle.
AI.result: First AI-creation of graphene; first AI-fabrication of complex nanodevices (atomically thin field-effect transistors via vdW stacking); demonstrated autonomous error correction and closed-loop experimentation for 2D materials creation and nano-processing.
AI.conclusion: Establishes a generalizable framework for self-improving embodied AI systems that learn directly from the quantum world, paving the way for accelerated discovery in quantum materials, electronics, and beyond.

title: Anomalous thermal and elastic properties of an epitaxial NiTi film exhibiting R-phase
summary: Shape memory alloys like NiTi are at the core of emerging thermal management applications, including elastocaloric refrigeration, thermoelastic harvesting, and latent heat storage. Most of these applications benefit from a small scale due to the accelerated heat exchange, but obtaining precise functional properties of films is challenging. Here we demonstrate that transient grating spectroscopy (TGS) enables characterization of elastic coefficients and thermal diffusivity of a 3 $μ$m thick epitaxial NiTi film during a thermally induced phase transformation. The in-situ measurement of a complete austenite$\rightarrow$R-phase$\rightarrow$martensite$\rightarrow$austenite temperature cycle reveals that the elastic properties exhibit a crossover of the shear moduli (from $c^\prime < c_{44}$ in austenite to $c^\prime > c_{44}$ in martensite) and that the thermal diffusivity changes by 450 $\%$ between the R-phase and austenite. This dramatic change, together with the absence of hysteresis between the R-phase and austenite, makes NiTi a promising material candidate for thermal switches. The results indicate that the change in thermal diffusivity originates from an anomalous heat capacity of the R-phase. Furthermore, our TGS study provides temperature-dependent thermal and elastic properties required for simulating thermal management microsystems using this material.

AI.tldr: This paper uses transient grating spectroscopy (TGS) to measure elastic coefficients and thermal diffusivity of a 3 μm thick epitaxial NiTi film during thermally induced phase transformation (austenite→R-phase→martensite→austenite). Key findings include a crossover of shear moduli, a 450% change in thermal diffusivity between R-phase and austenite, and the identification of NiTi as a promising candidate for thermal switches.
AI.motivation: Shape memory alloys like NiTi are key for emerging thermal management applications (elastocaloric refrigeration, thermoelastic harvesting, latent heat storage). Small-scale devices benefit from accelerated heat exchange, but obtaining precise functional properties of films is challenging, motivating the need for a characterization method.
AI.method: Transient grating spectroscopy (TGS) was used to characterize elastic coefficients and thermal diffusivity of a 3 μm thick epitaxial NiTi film in-situ during a complete thermally induced phase transformation cycle (austenite→R-phase→martensite→austenite).
AI.result: Elastic properties show a shear moduli crossover (c′ < c₄₄ in austenite → c′ > c₄₄ in martensite). Thermal diffusivity changes by 450% between R-phase and austenite with no hysteresis, attributed to anomalous heat capacity of the R-phase.
AI.conclusion: The dramatic, hysteresis-free thermal diffusivity change makes NiTi promising for thermal switches. TGS provides the temperature-dependent thermal and elastic properties needed for simulating thermal management microsystems using this material.

title: Universal interface fluctuations in absorbing-state phase transitions
summary: Despite similarities between models exhibiting absorbing phase transitions (APTs) and those showing Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) growth, the relationship between these universal fluctuations has remained elusive. We numerically study (1+1)-dimensional interfaces of (2+1)-dimensional models showing APTs of directed percolation (DP) and compact directed percolation (CDP) classes with an active boundary, finding a universal crossover from short-time APT-governed fluctuations to long-time KPZ fluctuations. Upon rescaling time and length by the APT correlation time and length, the cumulants of the interface height distributions collapse onto a single scaling function. The fluctuation properties of the discrete Domany-Kinzel model and the continuum stochastic Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov (sFKPP) equation coincide, indicating that the KPZ growth parameters are determined solely by fundamental properties of the APT. For the CDP sFKPP equation, a dimensionless parameter tunes both the critical interface distribution and the KPZ parameters, with the interface properties of the biased voter model recovered in a limiting case. These results uncover a universal crossover in which KPZ fluctuations emerge from APT fluctuations at long times, linking paradigmatic universality classes of nonequilibrium scale-invariant phenomena.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a universal crossover from short-time absorbing phase transition (APT) fluctuations to long-time Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) fluctuations in (1+1)-dimensional interfaces of (2+1)-dimensional APT models, linking these two paradigmatic nonequilibrium universality classes through scaling collapse and shared fluctuation properties.
AI.motivation: Despite known similarities between APT and KPZ models, the direct relationship between their universal fluctuations has remained elusive; this work aims to bridge these two fundamental nonequilibrium universality classes.
AI.method: Numerical study of (1+1)-dimensional interfaces in (2+1)-dimensional APT models (DP and CDP classes) with active boundaries, using the discrete Domany-Kinzel model and the continuum stochastic Fisher-Kolmogorov-Petrovsky-Piskunov (sFKPP) equation, with scaling analysis of interface height cumulants.
AI.result: A universal crossover from short-time APT-governed fluctuations to long-time KPZ fluctuations is found. Rescaled cumulants collapse onto a single scaling function. The sFKPP equation for CDP reveals a dimensionless parameter that tunes both the critical interface distribution and KPZ parameters.
AI.conclusion: KPZ fluctuations emerge universally from APT fluctuations at long times, establishing a fundamental link between these paradigmatic nonequilibrium scale-invariant phenomena, with APT properties determining KPZ growth parameters.

title: Spin and orbital mixing of edge states in a quantum Hall system proximitized by a superconductor
summary: We investigate the formation and transport properties of chiral Andreev edge states in a two-dimensional quantum Hall system proximitized by a superconductor. By numerically modeling the system using the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations, we analyze the non-local conductance and transmission probabilities of multimode and spinful systems. We demonstrate that the Andreev reflection process induces a mixing of the quantum Hall edge modes at higher filling factors, a phenomenon strictly prohibited in clean, purely electronic systems. When incorporating the Zeeman interaction, we show that the Andreev edge states split into uncoupled spin species, maintaining spin orthogonality that prevents mixing between opposite spin sectors. Furthermore, we explore the impact of Rashba spin-orbit coupling. While the spin-orbit interaction alone causes slight spin depolarization, its combination with an in-plane magnetic field drives complex spin mixing among all chiral Andreev bands, fundamentally altering the conductance oscillations. Finally, we reveal that the electron transmission probabilities exhibit robust degeneracies, which emerge as a direct consequence of the unitarity constraints and the particle-hole symmetry of the system's scattering matrix in a magnetic field and the presence of spin-orbit interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper studies chiral Andreev edge states in a 2D quantum Hall system proximitized by a superconductor, focusing on non-local conductance, Andreev-induced mode mixing, Zeeman splitting, Rashba spin-orbit coupling effects, and robust transmission degeneracies arising from unitarity and particle-hole symmetry.
AI.motivation: To understand the formation and transport properties of chiral Andreev edge states in hybrid quantum Hall-superconductor systems, particularly the mechanisms of mode mixing and spin dynamics that are absent in purely electronic systems.
AI.method: Numerical modeling using the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations to compute non-local conductance and transmission probabilities in multimode, spinful quantum Hall systems with superconducting proximity.
AI.result: Andreev reflection mixes quantum Hall edge modes at higher filling factors (forbidden in clean electronic systems); Zeeman interaction splits Andreev edge states into uncoupled spin species with preserved orthogonality; Rashba spin-orbit coupling alone causes slight spin depolarization, but combined with an in-plane magnetic field leads to complex spin mixing across all chiral Andreev bands; electron transmission probabilities exhibit robust degeneracies due to unitarity and particle-hole symmetry.
AI.conclusion: The interplay of Andreev reflection, Zeeman effect, and spin-orbit coupling in proximitized quantum Hall systems yields rich spin and mode mixing phenomena, with fundamental symmetry constraints governing transport properties.

title: Microstructure evolution during rapid solidification of hypoeutectic Al-Ag alloys near absolute stability
summary: Microsegregation-free microstructures can form by solidifying at velocities beyond the absolute stability limit ($V_{\text{abs}}$), where solute partitioning is suppressed by a stable, planar solid-liquid interface. Producing such microstructures is of considerable practical interest; however, $V_{\text{abs}}$ typically exceeds the ${\sim}1$ m/s growth rates encountered in additive manufacturing (AM). Here we demonstrate the absolute stability limit can be reached in sufficiently concentrated hypoeutectic Al-Ag alloys at growth rates well below the 1~m/s typically encountered in additive manufacturing. Dynamic Transmission Electron Microscopy (DTEM) of rapid solidification front evolution -- following laser spot melting of Al-Ag thin films -- combined with postmortem microstructural characterization, enables detailed quantitative comparison with both phase-field (PF) simulations and a sharp-interface linear stability analysis that uses a non-equilibrium, velocity-dependent phase diagram extracted from the PF model. The analysis predicts that $V_{\text{abs}}$ follows a trend similar to that of the miscibility gap, first increasing and then decreasing with Ag concentration. Predicted values of $V_{\text{abs}}$ are in good quantitative agreement with PF simulations over the entire hypoeutectic concentration range and with experiments for three concentrated alloys. These results inform the prediction and control of microstructural development in concentrated alloys near the absolute stability limit under AM conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the absolute stability limit for planar solidification can be reached in concentrated hypoeutectic Al-Ag alloys at growth rates below 1 m/s (typical in additive manufacturing) through experiments, phase-field simulations, and sharp-interface analysis. Predicted V_abs follows the miscibility gap trend and agrees well with both simulations and experiments.
AI.motivation: Microsegregation-free microstructures are practically desirable but typically require growth rates exceeding ~1 m/s (V_abs), which surpasses typical additive manufacturing rates. The authors aim to explore whether concentrated alloys can achieve absolute stability at lower, more accessible velocities.
AI.method: Dynamic Transmission Electron Microscopy (DTEM) was used to observe rapid solidification front evolution after laser spot melting of Al-Ag thin films. Postmortem microstructural characterization was combined with phase-field (PF) simulations and a sharp-interface linear stability analysis incorporating a non-equilibrium, velocity-dependent phase diagram extracted from the PF model.
AI.result: V_abs follows a trend similar to the miscibility gap: increasing then decreasing with Ag concentration. Predicted V_abs values show good quantitative agreement with PF simulations across the hypoeutectic range and with experimental data for three concentrated alloys.
AI.conclusion: Absolute stability can be achieved in concentrated Al-Ag alloys at growth rates well below 1 m/s, relevant to additive manufacturing conditions. This informs prediction and control of microstructural development near the absolute stability limit.

title: Network analysis for steady-state current fluctuations under finite affinity: Application to Brownian computation
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures, ancillary Mathematica notebook provided as supplemental material
summary: A graph-theoretic analysis of the steady-state current noise in master equations under a finite thermodynamic force (affinity) is presented. The incidence matrix twisted by a finite affinity is not orthogonal to the standard cycle space, motivating the introduction of twisted circuit matrices to restore the orthogonality. The resulting twisted-cycle matrix yields an interference-like effect, enabling us to express the signal-to-noise ratio as a quadratic optimization problem in terms of twisted-cycle currents. We apply this framework to a Brownian computation model on a tree-like state-transition diagram with exponential backward branching, finite affinity at each step, and a single reset cycle. In the limit of an infinitely long intended computation path $\ell$, the Fano factor of the reset current undergoes a transition from noiseless to Poissonian behavior at an affinity equal to the logarithm of the number of immediate predecessors $α$. This corresponds to an easy-hard transition in the computational time complexity [K. Okajima, K. Hukushima, arXiv:2512.24728 ], which is not captured by the thermodynamic uncertainty relation. This transition point precisely characterizes the thermodynamic costs of logically irreversible computation: in the absence of affinity, the reset cost scales as $\ln \ell$, whereas reaching the transition point requires a thermodynamic force of order $\ln α$ per step to counteract backward branching.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a graph-theoretic framework using twisted circuit matrices to analyze steady-state current noise in master equations under finite affinity, applying it to a Brownian computation model. It reveals a noise transition at affinity equal to log(α) corresponding to an easy-hard computational transition, with thermodynamic costs scaling differently below and at this transition.
AI.motivation: To analyze steady-state current noise in master equations under finite thermodynamic force (affinity) and understand the relationship between thermodynamic costs and computational complexity in logically irreversible computation.
AI.method: Graph-theoretic analysis using twisted circuit matrices to restore orthogonality lost due to finite affinity, expressing signal-to-noise ratio as a quadratic optimization problem over twisted-cycle currents.
AI.result: In the Brownian computation model, the Fano factor of reset current undergoes a noiseless-to-Poissonian transition at affinity = log(α). Without affinity, reset cost scales as ln(ℓ); at the transition point, thermodynamic force of order ln(α) per step is required.
AI.conclusion: The affinity-dependent noise transition corresponds to an easy-hard transition in computational time complexity not captured by thermodynamic uncertainty relations, precisely characterizing thermodynamic costs of logically irreversible computation.

title: Spin-caloritronic signatures of soft magnons in bilayer CrSBr
summary: Spin transport in magnetic insulators is often treated by assuming that magnons carry a fixed spin angular momentum of $\hbar$, which does not hold in general, however. Here we calculate the magnon spin angular momentum of a layered antiferromagnet as a function of applied magnetic field and wave vector. We show that the triaxial anisotropy and intralayer dipolar interactions in bilayer CrSBr renormalize the magnon spin angular momentum, which diverges upon field-induced magnon softening. This divergence gives rise to a pronounced peak in the thermal spin Seebeck response and provides a clear spin-caloritronic signature of soft magnons.

AI.tldr: The paper calculates magnon spin angular momentum in CrSBr, showing that triaxial anisotropy and dipolar interactions cause it to diverge at field-induced magnon softening, producing a distinct thermal spin Seebeck peak as a signature of soft magnons.
AI.motivation: The assumption that magnons carry a fixed spin angular momentum of $\hbar$ does not hold generally in magnetic insulators, motivating a more precise calculation of magnon spin angular momentum in layered antiferromagnets.
AI.method: The authors calculate the magnon spin angular momentum of a layered antiferromagnet (bilayer CrSBr) as a function of applied magnetic field and wave vector, incorporating triaxial anisotropy and intralayer dipolar interactions.
AI.result: Triaxial anisotropy and intralayer dipolar interactions renormalize the magnon spin angular momentum, which diverges upon field-induced magnon softening. This divergence produces a pronounced peak in the thermal spin Seebeck response.
AI.conclusion: The divergence in magnon spin angular momentum provides a clear spin-caloritronic signature of soft magnons.

title: A comparative first-principles investigation of bilayer NbOX2 (X=Cl, Br, I) for Photocatalytic water splitting applications
summary: Motivated by our previous work on bulk NbOX2 , where we have reported its high 1dielectric polarisation and finite piezoelectric response, this work extends to its 2D homo bilayer system to explore its potential for photocatalytic water splitting. Herein, density functional theory (DFT) were employed in probing the structural, electronic, optical, and photocatalytic properties of 2D homo bilayer NbOX2 (X = Cl, Br, and I). Our results show that structurally, NbOCl2 and NbOBr2 prefer AC bilayer stacking,while AB stacking was preferred by NbOI2 . All the considered bilayers are dynamically, thermally, and mechanically stable. From the analysis of electronic structure we have found a decreasing trend in the energy band gap as X goes down the group from Cl to I, with the position of the valence band maximum shifting upward along the high symmetry points. In terms of carrier mobility, all 2D bilayer systems possess high carrier mobility comparable to known 2D materials. It also exhibits an anisotropic carrier transfer property by which charge carriers are separated efficiently. These materials show similar trends to BiOI and PtSe2 , in which photocatalytic efficiency was increased by forming the multiple layers. The materials under investigation are suitable for photocatalytic water splitting under visible and ultraviolet regions with absorption coefficients of 105 cm-1.

AI.tldr: This DFT study investigates 2D homo bilayer NbOX₂ (X=Cl, Br, I) for photocatalytic water splitting, finding AC stacking for Cl/Br and AB stacking for I, with decreasing band gaps, high anisotropic carrier mobility, and strong visible-UV light absorption (~10⁵ cm⁻¹), suggesting suitability for photocatalysis.
AI.motivation: Extends previous work on bulk NbOX₂ (which showed high dielectric polarization and piezoelectric response) to 2D homo bilayer systems to explore their potential for photocatalytic water splitting.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) was used to probe structural, electronic, optical, and photocatalytic properties of 2D homo bilayer NbOX₂ (X = Cl, Br, I).
AI.result: NbOCl₂ and NbOBr₂ prefer AC bilayer stacking while NbOI₂ prefers AB stacking. Band gap decreases from Cl to I, with upward VBM shift. All systems show high, anisotropic carrier mobility comparable to known 2D materials, and absorption coefficients of ~10⁵ cm⁻¹ in visible and UV regions.
AI.conclusion: 2D bilayer NbOX₂ materials are dynamically, thermally, and mechanically stable, exhibit efficient charge carrier separation via anisotropic transport, and are suitable for photocatalytic water splitting under visible and UV light, similar to BiOI and PtSe₂ multi-layer systems.

title: Global resetting and emergent correlations: exit statistics in an interval
summary: There is considerable current interest in the emergence of statistical correlations within a population of otherwise non-interacting Brownian particles subject to a common fluctuating environment or drive. Examples include global stochastic resetting, switching confining potentials, fluctuating diffusivities, and stochastically gated boundaries. Most studies have focused on the analytical structure of the stationary joint probability density (assuming it exists). In this paper, we extend previous work on the exit statistics of multiple particles in stochastically gated domains to the case of global resetting in an interval with absorbing boundaries at both ends. First, we use a generalised Itô's lemma to derive a hierarchy of boundary value problems (BVPs) for the joint splitting probability that all particles exit from the same end of the interval. The BVPs form a nested sequence with respect to the initial number of particles $M$. We explicitly solve the BVP for a pair of particles ($M=2$) and use this to illustrate the emergence of pairwise correlations.
